articles.title: Who decides what constitutes dangerous artificial intelligence: the state or Nvidia? - Tomorrow's Affairs
articles.summary: Who decides what constitutes dangerous artificial intelligence: the state or Nvidia?  Tomorrow's Affairs
articles.full_text:
Jensen Huang, the founder and chief executive of Nvidia, the world’s leading artificial-intelligence chipmaker, said in an interview with Bloomberg Television on 14 October that Nvidia would suspend deliveries to any customer whose use of artificial intelligence would harm people.
He was responding to a hypothetical question and added that the decision would be preceded by a conversation with the customer, acknowledging that there are limits to a supplier’s right to impose its values on others.
Nvidia generated $89 billion in revenue from data-centre equipment alone in the quarter ended 26 July, and its chips power most of the world’s artificial-intelligence systems.
Any customer denied deliveries would struggle to find a replacement in the quantities required, so such a decision could effectively halt its development.
Nvidia is now linking the sale of its computing equipment to the development of safety tools and support for researchers examining AI safety.
Huang’s willingness to judge the harms caused by the use of its chips would extend that influence to the selection of eligible customers.
The company would therefore independently decide under which conditions the technology may spread, while its director claims that the industry does not need new laws.
China is the strongest test of Huang’s promise, as there is already a case there in which the state concluded that the sale of Nvidia’s chips posed a danger.
Washington has been restricting exports of the most advanced chips to China since 2022, fearing that they will be used to strengthen its military and to develop its own artificial intelligence capabilities.
In May 2025, Huang called the controls a failure, arguing that they merely help China’s competitors grow stronger.
His argument is supported by the latest data from research company IDC, which shows that Nvidia’s share of the Chinese market for artificial intelligence chips fell in the first half of 2026 to 34 per cent, while China’s Huawei reached 28 per cent.
Meanwhile, Washington relaxed but maintained controls. On 8 December 2025, President Donald Trump announced that Nvidia could sell H200 chips, the previous generation of its most powerful processors, to selected Chinese customers.
On 13 January 2026, the Department of Commerce mandated that each request be considered individually, with security requirements and mandatory chip testing in the United States.
Nvidia received the first licence, for limited quantities and specified customers, in February.
China shows how Nvidia reacts when the threat assessment comes from outside and starts to cost it money
The chips are manufactured in Taiwan, so before being shipped to China they must pass through the United States, where they are subject to a 25 per cent tariff. The US government thus takes a quarter of the value of each sale.
Beijing has not made it easy either, restricting domestic companies from buying American chips to encourage Huawei and other Chinese manufacturers.
That is why Nvidia delivered only a fraction of the approved quantities by the end of July, and those sales brought in less than 1 per cent of its data-centre equipment revenue.
Restrictions cost Nvidia money even when they are relaxed. In the same report, the company took a $400 million write-down because of an inventory of H200 chips that it could not sell.
When the US government banned the sale of H20 chips, a model made specifically for the Chinese market, in April 2025, Nvidia was left with stock it could no longer sell and recorded a loss of $4.5 billion.
Export controls concern the military and technological power of another country, and Huang’s October pledge concerns the harmful use of products, so the two cases are not quite the same.
China, however, shows how Nvidia reacts when the threat assessment comes from outside and starts to cost it money.
The company has the right to challenge government policy, but the argument that the restrictions do not work simultaneously protects its access to one of the world’s largest markets.
Huang’s announcement therefore carries no real weight until it is clear how much loss Nvidia would accept if the harmfulness of using its chips were decided by someone outside the company.
On 15 September, at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, the annual gathering of software company Salesforce, Huang said the industry “doesn’t need new laws or new regulations” and that AI security is an “engineering problem”.
Pope Leo XIV responded on 28 September at a press conference on the plane, on his way back from France.
He said he had read Huang’s claim that he had found a way to place technical limits on artificial intelligence and pointed out that this was the same man who said it did not need any restrictions or government regulation. Nvidia presented precisely that control system on the same day.
The Pope’s remark draws on the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, his letter on artificial intelligence published in May.
In it, he warns that decision-making is being concentrated in the hands of a small number of technology companies and insists that affected communities have a say. He specifically calls for legal frameworks and independent oversight.
The dispute with Huang thus centres on who sets the limits of artificial intelligence: the companies that create it, or the society that lives with its consequences.
Huang does not reject all state control, however. In a conversation with American journalist Ezra Klein at the end of September, he said that AI companies should not be exempt from competition laws or from responsibility for damage caused by their products.
He also supported special rules where needed, for example for autonomous cars.
The more secure agents become, the more companies will deploy them, and most of these agents will run on Nvidia chips
He draws the line at the models themselves, insisting that companies should decide whether a new artificial intelligence system is safe enough to enter the market.
Nvidia’s system is designed for so-called AI agents, programmes that autonomously perform a range of tasks, from sending emails to working with confidential company data.
The OpenShell programme determines which data and systems the agent is allowed to access, with rules set by the company that uses it.
Sentry, a dedicated hardware watchdog, monitors the agent’s operation and, according to Nvidia, can stop it within milliseconds if it tries to exceed the permitted limits.
The more secure agents become, the more companies will deploy them, and most of these agents will run on Nvidia chips. Protection is therefore a new way for Nvidia to sell more equipment.
Part of that offering is open. The OpenShell is publicly available and can be adapted to third-party equipment.
Sentry, however, runs only on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 hardware. A company that builds protection around both tools will be able to move software easily, but not monitoring, so switching to another supplier will become increasingly expensive as it relies more on Nvidia’s equipment.
Nvidia announced that it will provide British artificial intelligence security researchers with computing capacity worth an estimated $250 million, or about $50 million per year, over the next five years.
That funding will remain within Nvidia’s system, as universities gain the right to use the computers of its British partners, equipped with its chips.
Among the first users will be the BOLD laboratory at Oxford and the SOFAIR laboratory, UK national AI research laboratory.
The announcement explicitly states that researchers will also work with the OpenShell and Sentry tools.
In the coming years, British security experts will, at Nvidia’s expense, examine and improve the very protections that Nvidia sells to companies
In the coming years, British security experts will, at Nvidia’s expense, examine and improve the very protections that Nvidia sells to companies.
Universities will receive equipment for costly experiments that they could hardly fund themselves, and Nvidia will gain the opportunity to establish its solutions as a common benchmark for assessing the safety of artificial intelligence.
Key terms have not yet been agreed. Nvidia has not announced which partners will provide the services, how the computers will be organised, under what commercial terms, or how much individual universities will receive.
Those contracts will also depend on whether researchers are allowed to freely publish findings that are unfavourable to the donor.
Part of the programme could also work against Nvidia’s interests. The SOFAIR laboratory investigates new ways of building artificial intelligence, with the aim that development does not depend on a few large companies.
Nvidia’s funding could therefore support technologies that may one day reduce dependence on its products, provided the results can be used on other organisations’ equipment.
The British package seems more modest than the American one. On 8 October, Nvidia announced $1 billion over five years for US science, health, energy and advanced computing research – four times more than for Britain.
However, Britain is not tied to a single supplier. Nvidia’s main competitor, AMD, announced in June that it would invest up to two billion pounds over five years in British computing infrastructure and scientific collaboration, and it is also participating in Oxford’s BOLD laboratory.
This freedom of choice has its price, because every programme written for one set of equipment must be adapted before switching to another, and that price increases with each year of operation on the same chips.
The British government has its own institute to evaluate artificial intelligence, but it has no authority to examine systems without the consent of the companies that develop them.
The AI Security Institute was founded in November 2023, at the first world summit on artificial intelligence safety at Bletchley Park, under the name AI Safety Institute.

articles.title: TSMC's AI Chip Bottleneck Grows as Nvidia, Apple Scramble for Wafers - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: TSMC's AI Chip Bottleneck Grows as Nvidia, Apple Scramble for Wafers  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) just delivered its sixth straight quarter of record profit, yet the numbers tell only half the story. Behind the earnings beat lies a supply squeeze so severe that the world's largest contract chipmaker is fielding desperate calls from customers, weighing which tech giants get priority access to scarce wafers, and watching rivals circle for the overflow.
The company posted net income of NT$763.1 billion (approximately $23.5 billion) for the July-to-September period, a 69% jump from a year earlier and ahead of the NT$746.3 billion consensus estimate compiled by LSEG from 16 analysts. Revenue reached $46.7 billion, up 16.2% sequentially and above the high end of its own guidance.
Gross margin slipped 1.3 percentage points to 66.4%, a decline the company attributed partly to the early ramp-up of its 2-nanometer production. High-performance computing revenue surged 22% from the prior quarter and now accounts for 68% of total sales. Chips built on 7-nanometer and more advanced nodes represented 79% of wafer revenue.
The earnings call, scheduled for 0600 GMT, will draw intense scrutiny from investors already rattled by the Federal Reserve's rate signals. TSMC's Taipei-listed shares closed down 2% on Thursday before the release, while the benchmark index fell 3.4%.
Customers Compete for Limited Capacity
The scramble for TSMC's manufacturing slots has become one of the defining dynamics of the AI infrastructure buildout. Jordan Klein, managing director at Mizuho Securities, told CNBC that competition is especially intense among heavyweight customers including Broadcom, NVIDIA (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD).
Sajiv Dalal, president of TSMC North America, said he receives at least 10 calls daily from customers seeking wafer capacity. Klein estimated the company could expand output by 10% to 20% beyond earlier targets, potentially reaching 120,000 wafers per month by year-end. He expects NVIDIA and Apple to capture a large portion of any additional supply.
TSMC's customer concentration underscores the stakes. Its 10 largest clients accounted for 78% of 2025 net revenue, according to CNBC.
Packaging Becomes Another Chokepoint
Wafer production is not the only constraint. Advanced packaging, particularly TSMC's chip-on-wafer-on-substrate technology known as CoWoS, has emerged as a separate bottleneck. Vlad Galabov, co-host of The AIDC Debate, said NVIDIA has already reserved most of the company's CoWoS capacity, and TSMC is working to double that capability to satisfy demand for AI processors.
Klein noted that rather than waiting for entirely new factories, TSMC could accelerate output by installing additional equipment at existing facilities. The company is expanding in Taiwan, Japan, and Arizona, has committed to ASML Holding's (ASML) $400 million High-NA EUV technology, and is reportedly evaluating another manufacturing site in Texas.
The capital intensity is enormous. TSMC raised its 2026 capex forecast in July to between $60 billion and $64 billion, up from a prior outlook at the top end of $52 billion to $56 billion. The company is investing $265 billion to build chip plants in Arizona, including an additional $100 billion announced in July.
Shortages Threaten AI Roadmaps
The constraints could disrupt the technology industry's aggressive AI expansion plans. Klein warned that shortages of advanced logic chips could threaten ambitious revenue projections for frontier AI models and large-scale infrastructure projects.
Galabov distinguished the logic chip shortage from memory constraints, explaining that processors require customized designs and long-term production planning. That structural rigidity means even marquee customers such as NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple face supply risks.
Sid Sheth of dMatrix said TSMC evaluates potential customers based on long-term demand forecasts, target markets, and expected production requirements rather than immediate orders alone. The company remains highly selective, expecting credible demand projections from any would-be partner.
Rivals Position for Share
TSMC's constraints could open doors for Intel (INTC) and Samsung Electronics (OTC: SSNLF), which are positioning themselves as alternative manufacturing partners. Klein said Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is working to strengthen the company's manufacturing operations and attract external foundry customers. Potential clients could include Apple, NVIDIA, and companies linked to Elon Musk, though such arrangements remain speculative.
Tesla's CEO said last week that his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing part of it. Reuters reported in September that TSMC was evaluating a potential investment in Texas.
ASML offered a bullish signal on Wednesday, saying customers were already placing orders for 2029 and 2030, easing concerns that the AI investment cycle was losing momentum.
TSMC's market capitalization now stands at roughly $2 trillion, nearly double that of Samsung Electronics. Its Taipei-listed shares have gained 57% so far in 2026, roughly in line with the broader Taiwanese market's 62% advance. U.S.-listed shares have climbed nearly 40%, trailing the PHLX Semiconductor Index's 60% rise.
For now, AI demand continues to reinforce TSMC's dominant position in advanced chip manufacturing. The company's earnings streak shows no sign of breaking, but the capacity ceiling it faces is becoming the entire industry's problem.

articles.summary: GTA 6 Launch Trailer Analysis: Has a Long-Standing Tech Issue Been Fixed?  Digital FoundryGrand Theft Auto VI Launch Trailer  Rockstar GamesJustice Created the Score for ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’: Hear the Duo’s New Song With Tame Impala, SZA & More  BillboardGrand Theft Auto VI Gets A Final, Salacious Trailer  Game InformerGTA 6 fans spot mysterious detail at 0:55 in new trailer  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Rockstar released Grand Theft Auto 6's launch trailer yesterday, granting a precious 90 seconds of (mostly new) video of the upcoming juggernaut. We've now had a chance to analyse the video, and though it's impossible to say for sure, the footage suggests that a big issue we spotted with the game in earlier trailers has been fixed.
In short, the previous GTA 6 trailers have all demonstrated some animation pacing errors, where camera movements and character animations can appear jerky even when the game's overall frame-rate looks stable. This has been an unfortunate feature of past RAGE engine titles since Grand Theft Auto 4, so it wasn't a surprise to see it in the GTA 6 footage too.
In the new launch trailer, that characteristic inconsistency isn't present, including in slow pans and other shots where it would normally be visible. This is only a short trailer, of course, and Rockstar could have shot the video in a way that doesn't reveal the problem as overtly, but it could also suggest that this long-standing tech oddity has finally been fixed - assuming that the footage here is representative of the game. This was one of the two major issues we identified in the Extended Look footage, so seeing it seemingly solved is exciting.
Elsewhere, the trailer is classic Rockstar, with creative camera work, a huge range of different scenes and effects, and one that demonstrates the mastery of subtle phonomena, like the way that water droplets catch the sunlight and react against chest hair in the shower scene. It's fair to say that the entire video is lushly presented, even down to the extremely detailed iguana shown in the opening seconds of the trailer - which looks to have finally exceeded the herpetofaunal representation in similarly graphics-focused titles like Cyberpunk 2077 and Crysis 3.
We also wanted to draw attention to some thoughts on the game's possible HDR presentation thanks to Filippo Tarpini, an HDR specialist that is best known for their work at game developer Remedy. Tarpini suspects that Rockstar might be using the AGX tone mapper, which could account for some colour shifts in the footage, such as blue light appearing purplish. There are also hints that Rockstar is using inverse tone mapping to create an HDR presentation from SDR-like material, but this is only an informed guess - we'll have to wait until we get solid information or see the game for ourselves to deliver a verdict on the HDR implementation.
One of the biggest questions surrounding the trailer is over whether it uses the new QSSR technique that Sony unveiled recently, bringing AI-based upscaling from the PS5 Pro to the base PS5. From our point of view, it's not clear one way or another, but we'd probably lean towards QSSR not being used - as the image quality did look good, but the cinematic shots used here just might have been selected to avoid the aliasing and image quality issues that were more prominent in the Extended Look trailer.
Again, the resolution here looks to be 1440p upscaled to 4K (albeit with black bars), and based on our testing of QSSR in Wolverine that kind of upscale seems to have a cost of around 4ms - which would be a lot of the 33ms budget to spend on upscaling, when 1440p is already a relatively high resolution. But really, we've seen so little of QSSR so far, we really need to see more titles to get to grips with its rendering cost and quality.
Overall, the launch trailer is another good indicator of how supremely polished the game is looking at this late stage. What we'd like to see is some kind of affirmation as to why the game is "best on PS5" and indeed what buyers should expect on each launch platform, as right now we can only speculate as to how features, image quality and performance will vary across the four consoles.
For now though, we'll leave it there. Stay tuned for more GTA 6 analysis as more materials are (hopefully) released in the run-up to launch on November 19th.

The "Best on PS5" is of course just marketing bought by Sony, but at the same time, it will play "best" there by default just because of PS5 Pro. Even if the Pro had like zero enhancements made to it at all, just the extra little bit of CPU clockspeed and more graphics horsepower would still provide better framerate stability, therefore still making it the "best" way to play.
I'm sure GTA VI will be all but identical on base PS5/Xbox Series X, with Series S bringing up the rear and PS5 Pro sitting on top. At least until the PC version releases.

articles.title: Screen use, artificial intelligence and social media: Impact on children and young people - House of Lords Library
articles.summary: Screen use, artificial intelligence and social media: Impact on children and young people  House of Lords Library
articles.full_text:
Approximate read time: 35 minutes
The House of Lords is scheduled to debate the following motion on 22 October 2026:
Lord Patel (Crossbench) to move that this House takes note of the effect of artificial intelligence, screen usage and social media on children.
1. Key points
- Children and young people are increasingly using screens and online services such as AI (particularly generative AI) and social media. The sector regulator Ofcom has found that the two most popular activities for children are playing video games and watching TV and films.
- Screen use among some children, particularly high screen use, has been linked to issues including developmental and behavioural issues, poor sleep, sedentary behaviour and exposure to online harms (such as cyberbullying and grooming). Children aged under five are particularly vulnerable to developmental issues from screen use. However, screen use can bring some benefits, particularly when the use is ‘active’ (when adults or others are involved in the activity). Evidence shows that some screen use can be beneficial for learning and development.
- In a 2025 report, Ofcom found that over two-thirds of children aged three to 17 were reportedly using social media apps. Many children used social media despite being under the age limit for the platform (often set at 13). Although social media was found to bring some benefits, such as helping form networks with other young people with common interests or experiences, it was often found to have certain ‘addictive’ design elements. Social media use by young people has been linked to issues including mental health challenges, poor sleep and exposure to harassment and abuse.
- Evidence of young people’s use of AI is an emerging area. Ofcom reported that young people may use AI for education support, creative outputs and companionship. Evidence of its impact on young people was mixed, with possible benefits and drawbacks to its effect on education, development and health and wellbeing. However, young people have raised concerns about its potential impact on their lives and future careers. In addition, there are concerns about people illegally using AI to create deepfakes or sexualised images of children.
- The Online Safety Act 2023 requires certain online platforms, including social media platforms and sites hosting pornographic content, to take measures to prevent children from accessing harmful and age-inappropriate content. The government has also announced that it will legislate to ban under-16s from using social media. It has also said it will introduce other laws and restrictions intended to make children’s use of online spaces, AI and social media safer; for example, by restricting some of the ‘addictive’ design elements of social media and requiring in-app or device-level protections. Many, including parents, are supportive of the ban and other proposed changes. However, there are some concerns children will try to bypass the ban and may therefore end up using less regulated spaces.
2. How much do children and young people use this technology?
2.1 Overview of screen use
Research has found increasing screen and technology use by children and young people.[1] According to statistics published by Ofcom in May 2026, on average:[2]
- children aged eight to nine spent just under three hours online each day
- children aged 10 to 12 spent around three and a half hours online each day
- children aged 13 to 14 spent around four hours and 20 minutes online each day
In terms of device usage, Ofcom has separately found that:
Just under eight in 10 (78%) children aged 8–17 have their own mobile phone, six in 10 (59%) use a tablet to go online, and 55% use a games console. Ownership of a mobile phone rises sharply from 56% of 10-year-olds to more than eight in 10 (83%) of 11-year-olds. Nearly all (98%) 16–17s own a mobile phone.[3]
Activities involving screen use were found to be the most popular among young people, with playing video games and watching TV the most mentioned. However, sport and spending time with friends and family also ranked in the top six:
Figure 1. Ofcom findings on children and young people’s self-reported favourite activities (ordered by % that listed that activity)
Commenting further on children’s use of screens and the internet, Ofcom found:
The internet is central to most children’s lives, with parents saying that 88% of children aged 3–7, and almost all (99%) children aged 8–17 go online. Over half (55%) of children aged 3–17 play games online.
[…]
91% of children aged 4–15 watched some type of audio-visual content on a weekly basis in 2025. Over six in 10 (63%) 4–15s watched some broadcast TV on a weekly basis in 2025, down from 66% in 2024. Time spent viewing of YouTube and other video-sharing platforms (VSPs) increased by 3% between 2024 and 2025, and VSPs account for the largest share of children’s in-home video viewing […][4]
Ofcom also looked into the use of screens among children aged under two for the first time in 2026. Its survey found that 65% of parents of children aged six months to two years said their child went online (mostly through smart TVs or tablets) and 85% said their child sometimes “looks at a screen”.[5] Reasons given by parents for this screen use included:
- to provide entertainment: 67%
- to support learning: 63%
- because their child enjoys it: 52%
- to occupy their child while they carry out other tasks: 49%
The following graphic shows the screen time activities of those aged under two years:
Figure 2. Ofcom findings on how children under two years use screens
2.2 Social media use
Ofcom’s reports on children’s media usage have found increasing use of social media by children and young people, including in younger age groups. In its 2026 report, it found that:[6]
- among eight to 14-year-olds, 54% had used TikTok, 43% had used Snapchat, 34% had used Instagram and 33% had used Facebook in the past four weeks
- for 15 to 17-year-olds, 69% had used TikTok, 63% had used Snapchat, 62% had used Instagram and 54% had used Facebook in the previous four weeks
However, Ofcom also found the majority of eight to 17-year-olds who used social media stated they were ‘passive’ users (65%); for example, they mainly read, watched, followed or ‘liked’ social media content. Around a third (34%) said they were ‘active’ users, where they would share, comment on or post content.
In its 2025 report, Ofcom found that over two-thirds (68%) of children aged three to 17 were reportedly using social media apps, including 55% of three to 5-year-olds.[7] Commenting further on the prevalence of social media use, Ofcom said:
More than a third (36%) of parents of 3–5s whose child uses at least one social media app or site state that they use social media on their child’s behalf, and over four in 10 (42%) say they use these sites or apps together with their child. However, a further two in 10 (19%) parents of 3–5s who use social media say that their child uses these apps independently.
[…]
Eight in 10 of all children (79%) aged 3–17 have their own profile on at least one VSP
, messaging or livestreaming app, or social media site. While seven in 10 3–12-year-olds have at least one such profile, this is almost universal among teens; 97% of 13–17s report that they have at least one profile on these types of sites or app. When focusing on social media apps/sites alone, four in 10 (40%) under-13s have a profile on this type of service.
The younger group (3-12s) are most likely to have a profile on YouTube/YouTube Kids (44%), WhatsApp (23%) and/or TikTok (23%), while 13–17s are most likely to have profiles on WhatsApp (62%), Snapchat (62%) or TikTok (61%).
[…]
Four in 10 (37%) parents of 3–17s said they would allow their child to have a profile on social media sites or apps before they had reached the minimum age requirement. Agreement with this statement was highest among parents of 10–12-year-olds, at 50%.[8]
Most social media companies set a minimum age requirement of 13 for using their service. In addition, the Online Safety Act 2023 requires social media companies to enforce any age limits consistently and protect child users.[9]
2.3 Use of artificial intelligence
In its 2026 report on children’s media use, Ofcom reported increasing use of AI (particularly generative AI such as ChatGPT and CoPilot) by young people. It found that 35% of eight to nine-year-olds said they have used AI and reported use by 12 to 17-year-olds was between 63% and 68%.[10] In addition, the report found:
- around half of eight to 17-year-olds said they use AI for schoolwork or homework (an increase on previous years)
- it was often used for fun or to help with doing creative activities online
- one in 10 AI users aged eight to 17 said they have used AI as someone to talk to or ‘as a friend’
- there was a gap between children’s confidence and their ability to recognise whether images are real or AI-generated
- four in 10 teenagers who are aware of AI said they would trust an AI‑generated article either more than, or to the same extent as, a human‑written article
- nearly half (46%) of eight to 17-year-olds who have read AI summaries in internet search results believe the information is always accurate
3. How is the technology used and what is the impact?
3.1 Screen use
As set out above, activities involving screen use are increasingly common in children’s lives. As noted in Ofcom’s 2026 report on children’s online experiences, this can involve a range of devices and activities:
Almost all 8–17-year-olds are online (99%) and most (78%) have their own mobile phone—with ownership rising steeply between age 10 and 11 (56% to 83%). articles.title: Future of Artificial Intelligence: Business, Jobs & Society - Business Outreach Magazine
articles.summary: Future of Artificial Intelligence: Business, Jobs & Society  Business Outreach Magazine
articles.full_text:
A decade ago, most executives treated artificial intelligence as a research curiosity buried inside university labs and a handful of technology giants. That has changed faster than almost anyone predicted. Boardrooms, classrooms, hospitals, and government offices are now asking the same question: what does the Future of Artificial Intelligence actually look like for the way we work, earn, and live?
Nobody has a complete picture yet, but the direction of travel is getting clearer every quarter. AI future trends now point toward a workplace where generative AI, machine learning, and autonomous AI agents sit alongside human judgement rather than replacing it outright. This article looks at what is realistic, what is overhyped, and what businesses, employees, and policymakers should actually be preparing for.
Quick Glance
| Dimension | What the data shows | Why it matters | 
| Business productivity | 88% of organisations use AI in at least one business function (McKinsey, 2026) | Automation of routine tasks frees teams for higher-value work | 
| Jobs and employment | WEF’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 projects 170 million roles created and 92 million displaced by 2030 | Net job creation still leads, but the transition is uneven across sectors | 
| Enterprise scaling | Only around 21% of adopters have redesigned a workflow around AI (McKinsey, 2026) | Adoption without redesign limits real productivity returns | 
| Global exposure | Nearly 40% of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI-driven change (IMF, January 2026) | Advanced economies face the steepest near-term exposure | 
| Human-AI collaboration | 66% of AI-using U.S. businesses use AI to augment tasks, not replace staff | Augmentation, not elimination, is the dominant pattern in 2026 | 
The Future of Artificial Intelligence
Strip away the marketing and the Future of Artificial Intelligence is less about humanoid robots and more about software that gets better at specific tasks every few months. Generative AI models now write code, draft contracts, summarise meetings, and generate marketing copy in a fraction of the time a human team would need.
AI agent systems that can plan, use tools, and complete multi-step tasks with limited supervision are the next layer of this shift. Analysts expect task-specific AI agents to appear in roughly 40% of enterprise applications by the end of 2026, which is really what the future of AI technology comes down to at this stage: narrower, more capable tools stacking on top of one another.
None of this means every job disappears overnight. It means the boundary between ‘human work’ and ‘AI-assisted work’ keeps moving, and companies that track artificial intelligence trends 2026 closely tend to adapt faster than those that wait for certainty that is unlikely to arrive.
How AI Will Change Business
The clearest place to see the Future of Artificial Intelligence take shape right now is inside day-to-day business operations.
AI and Business Productivity
The clearest AI impact on business so far is productivity. McKinsey’s State of AI research found that 88% of organisations now use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year earlier. Most of that use is still narrow: drafting text, summarising documents, automating customer queries, but even narrow automation compounds over time.
A support team that resolves routine tickets through an AI agent frees senior staff for complex escalations. A finance team that automates reconciliation spends more time on forecasting instead of data entry. The productivity gain rarely comes from one dramatic overhaul; it comes from dozens of small, unglamorous tasks quietly handed to software.
Personalised Customer Experiences
Recommendation engines, dynamic pricing, and AI chatbots have moved from novelty to default. Retailers use machine learning to personalise offers in real time, and customer service teams increasingly route first-contact queries to AI agents before a human ever gets involved.
Done well, this shortens wait times and improves resolution rates. Done poorly, it frustrates customers who feel funnelled through a script with no way out. The businesses getting this right treat AI as a first filter, not a replacement for a human safety net.
AI-Powered Decision-Making
Executives increasingly use AI-generated forecasts, risk scores, and scenario models to support decisions that used to rely on gut instinct and static spreadsheets. This does not remove human judgement from the process; it changes what that judgement is applied to.
Instead of manually building a demand forecast, a manager now reviews and adjusts one, then decides how to act on it. That shift, repeated across thousands of decisions a year, is a quiet but significant part of digital transformation inside large organisations.
New AI-Based Business Models
Some companies are going further and building entire products around AI rather than adding AI to existing ones. Subscription tools that offer an AI co-pilot for a specific profession legal research, radiology review, code review are growing quickly because they solve a narrow, well-defined problem better than a general-purpose chatbot.
That kind of AI impact on business rarely shows up in a single flashy launch. It shows up gradually, as one vertical AI tool after another chips away at a task that used to need a specialist and several hours. Expect more industry-specific AI products through 2026 and beyond, rather than one dominant do-everything assistant.
How AI Will Change Jobs
AI and jobs is the part of this conversation that understandably worries people most, and the honest picture is mixed rather than catastrophic.
Automation and Job Displacement
The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 projects that AI and related technologies could lead to significant job losses, displacing around 92 million roles globally by 2030 while creating approximately 170 million new jobs.
Goldman Sachs’ 2026 analysis found the U.S. losing a net 16,000 jobs a month to AI, a meaningful number but far from a labour-market collapse. What is more consistent across research is that data on AI and jobs increasingly shows suppressed hiring rather than mass firing; companies are slower to post entry-level roles, particularly in software development and back-office finance, even where existing staff are not let go.
New AI-Related Careers
Roles that did not exist five years ago prompt engineers, AI governance specialists, machine learning operations staff, and AI ethics reviewers are now standard job postings at mid-sized companies, not just at big technology firms.
LinkedIn data cited by the World Economic Forum shows the global economy added 1.3 million new AI-related jobs over a two-year period. These roles reward people who understand both the technology and the business problem it is solving, which is a different skill set than pure software engineering.
AI Skills and Reskilling
AI skills and literacy are becoming as basic a workplace expectation as spreadsheet literacy was two decades ago.. Employers increasingly expect staff to know how to prompt, verify, and edit AI output rather than write everything from a blank page.
Critical thinking matters more, not less, in this environment, because someone still has to catch the AI’s mistakes. Communication, creativity, and leadership skills the ones AI still struggles to replicate convincingly are becoming the difference between employees displaced by workforce transformation and those promoted because of it.
The Rise of Human-AI Collaboration
The most realistic reading of the data is that most workplaces are heading toward augmentation rather than replacement. Research on U.S. businesses using AI found that 66% use it solely to support existing tasks, and only about 2% report AI-related headcount reductions.
That does not mean displacement is not happening in specific roles. Customer support, junior coding, and basic content writing have all seen real pressure, but at an economy-wide level, human-AI collaboration is the dominant pattern in 2026, not human replacement. The most effective teams treat AI as a fast, tireless junior colleague: good at drafts, data pulls, and repetition, but still needing a human to set direction, catch errors, and take responsibility for the outcome.
How AI Will Change Society
Beyond the office, AI in society is already showing up in hospitals, classrooms, and daily commutes, often in ways people barely notice.
Healthcare
AI already supports diagnostic imaging review, drug discovery, and administrative workloads inside hospitals, and physician adoption of AI tools has crossed the halfway mark in several health systems. The realistic near-term impact is fewer diagnostic errors and faster paperwork, not AI doctors replacing human ones.
Education
Education has one of the highest generative AI adoption rates of any sector, driven by tools that help students draft, summarise, and self-test. Teachers are using AI to prepare lesson plans and personalise material for different learning speeds, though concerns about over-reliance on AI-written work remain a live debate in most school systems.
Transportation
Autonomous and semi-autonomous vehicle technology continues to expand in pilot cities, and AI-driven logistics is already reducing delivery times and fuel costs for large fleets. Full driverless transport at scale is further out than some coverage suggests, but AI-optimised routing and fleet management are already mainstream.
Everyday Life
Voice assistants, AI-generated recommendations, and automated scheduling tools are now background infrastructure for millions of people rather than novelties. The future of AI technology in daily life looks less like dramatic new gadgets and more like existing apps quietly getting smarter.
Risks and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence
This is the part of the Future of Artificial Intelligence that deserves a balanced look rather than either panic or dismissal.

articles.title: [进展] Prediction: $1,000 Invested in Taiwan Semi (TSMC) Today Will Be Worth This Much by 2030. - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: Prediction: $1,000 Invested in Taiwan Semi (TSMC) Today Will Be Worth This Much by 2030.  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
Over the past four years, a $1,000 investment in TSMC (TSM -2.28%), the world's largest contract chipmaker, would have grown to about $4,540. That multibagger gain was primarily driven by the rapid growth of the cloud infrastructure and AI markets.
Could a fresh $1,000 investment in TSMC grow to more than $4,500 again by the end of the decade? Let's review its catalysts, challenges, and valuations to see if it's possible.
Understanding TSMC's core advantages
TSMC manufactures the world's smallest, densest, and most power-efficient chips for fabless chipmakers like Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%), AMD, and Broadcom. To maintain its lead over other foundries, TSMC purchases more extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems -- which are required for optically etching tiny circuit patterns onto silicon wafers -- from ASML (ASML -0.96%) than any other foundry.
Once a fabless chipmaker is locked into TSMC's manufacturing services, the astronomical switching costs prevent it from moving to a competing foundry such as Samsung or Intel (INTC -5.79%). TSMC also offers a higher yield (the percentage of functional chips per wafer) than other foundries. So while TSMC's competitors might offer lower manufacturing costs per wafer, their lower yields and tighter production bottlenecks can easily offset those savings.
TSMC's scale enables it to push ASML's current-gen "low-NA" EUV systems to their theoretical limits (to 1.4nm) before it needs to buy ASML's pricier "high-NA" EUV systems to produce even smaller chips. By comparison, Intel is making the leap to high-NA much earlier than TSMC -- but that expansion will be costly because those systems cost about twice as much as low-NA systems. By waiting until the early 2030s to ramp up its purchases of high-NA EUV systems, TSMC can wait for the technology to mature and become cheaper before making that leap.
In the third quarter of 2026, TSMC generated 68% of its revenue from the high-performance computing (HPC) market -- which includes Nvidia's data center GPUs and Broadcom's custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) for hyperscalers.
That segment's revenue surged 22% sequentially in the third quarter, accelerating from 20% sequential growth in the first and second quarters. That acceleration should continue as long as more companies upgrade their cloud and AI data centers. It also generated a third of its revenue from its smallest 3nm chips -- which include Nvidia's Vera Rubin (Vera CPU and Rubin GPU) chips and the base die of the latest high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips.
How much bigger could TSMC grow?
Back in January, TSMC expected its revenue to grow in the mid-to-high 20% range in USD terms for the full year. But it raised its outlook to over 30% growth in its first-quarter report, just over 40% in its second-quarter report, and 44% in its third-quarter report. It kept raising its guidance to reflect the feverish growth of the generative AI market.
For 2026, analysts expect its revenue and EPS to rise 46% and 66%, respectively, in TWD terms. From 2026 to 2028, they expect its revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 32% and 31%, respectively. Yet TSMC's stock still looks cheap at 16 times next year's earnings.
If TSMC matches analysts' expectations through 2028, grows its EPS at a 25% CAGR for the next three years, and trades at 20 times forward earnings by late 2030, its stock could turn $1,000 into over $3,000. That wouldn't match its performance over the past four years, but it would still beat the S&P 500's (^GSPC -1.09%) average annual total return of about 10%.
TSMC might face unpredictable challenges over the next few years, including conflicts between Taiwan and China, the costly construction of its overseas plants (especially in the U.S.), and an abrupt slowdown in AI spending. But over the long term, it will likely remain a linchpin of the global semiconductor market -- and it should generate impressive gains for its patient investors.

articles.title: Amid TSMC-Terafab Talks, Taiwan Said To Be Mulling Greater Curbs On AI Chip Sales To China - TradingView
articles.summary: Amid TSMC-Terafab Talks, Taiwan Said To Be Mulling Greater Curbs On AI Chip Sales To China  TradingView
articles.full_text:
- Taiwan plans to bring AI chip and server export rules closer to U.S. restrictions.
- TSMC is discussing a potential role in Musk’s Terafab project as it invests $265 billion in U.S. chip manufacturing.
- TSMC expects quarterly sales growth of 61% after reporting a 51% jump in Q3 revenue, easing concerns about AI chip demand.
Taiwan is preparing to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips and servers shipped to China, bringing its rules closer to U.S. restrictions, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing a senior official in Taipei.
Taiwan’s Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin told Bloomberg News in an interview earlier this week that the government plans to add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its list of controlled items.
Once the new rules take effect, unauthorized shipments of restricted AI hardware to China would become a criminal offense under Taiwan’s Foreign Trade Act. He did not provide a timeline for implementation.
Taiwan is home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), the world’s biggest contract chip-maker and a key producer of Nvidia chips.
Despite U.S. restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia processors have continued to reach Chinese buyers through alleged smuggling networks operating across Southeast Asia.
Taiwan does not currently treat unauthorized AI chip exports to China as a criminal offense, and the proposed measures would significantly tighten Taipei’s enforcement efforts, according to the report.
Taiwan’s TSMC Grows US Presence
The development comes as TSMC is pouring $265 billion into setting up chip-making operations in the U.S. amid a push from U.S. President Donald Trump to bring advanced chip manufacturing onshore. TSMC is also exploring a partnership with Elon Musk’s Terafab project, TSMC CEO C.C. Wei and Musk have confirmed.
“We are still in discussion, let me say that,” Wei told analysts on TSMC’s analyst call following its results release on Thursday, referring to discussion with Musk over Terafab. “But the fab has got to be run by TSMC.”
The comments came a week after Musk appeared to rule out an operational role for the Taiwanese chipmaker at Terafab. Musk had said his companies would build and operate the facility themselves, adding that TSMC could potentially sublease part of the planned site but would not run its manufacturing operations.
TSMC separately confirmed a Reuters report saying it is considering fabs in Texas but offered no new information.
TSMC Q3 Results
TSMC projected 61% sales growth for the ongoing quarter this week, after posting a 51% rise in Q3 sales that topped Wall Street expectations.
With semiconductor firms ASML Holding NV and Samsung Electronics also reporting strong results in recent weeks, TSMC's report allayed fears of a slowdown in AI-led chip demand.
“We have not modeled the purported Texas cluster as nothing has been agreed yet, but long-term upside is enormous. We estimate matching the full scale of Tesla's Terafab would triple TSMC's effective capacity,” Morningstar analysts said in their note.
The research firm maintained its price target of T$3,440 and $534 on the Taipei- and U.S.-listed shares, respectively.

Roughly 30% of PhD dissertations in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) in the United States this year contained AI-generated text, according to a working paper1 that reviewed the abstracts submitted to an online database since 2019.
What’s more, the working paper, which has not been peer reviewed, found that PhD graduates who use artificial intelligence to help write their dissertations are more likely to work in industry and less likely to enter academia.
Various studies have shown a marked increase in the presence of text generated using AI in scientific literature over the past few years. Researchers at the US-based non-profit organization the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) wanted to understand how PhD students use AI because insights into students’ training and capabilities will shape science over the next several decades.
“If our students are only doing half the work and they’re dishing the rest to AI, do they really have the depth of understanding” to be good scientists? asks co-author Daniel Gross, an economist at NBER who is based in Durham.
The working paper analysed dissertations from more than 226,000 STEM doctoral graduates completed between January 2019 and May 2026 at US universities. The team used the AI-detection service Pangram to assess the abstracts. For the study, the researchers categorized abstracts as either AI-written or not; they did not distinguish between text that was wholly or partly generated by AI. (Although Gross says that 90% of the flagged AI-generated abstracts were classified by Pangram as entirely AI-generated.)
The team found that AI-generated text in dissertation abstracts first appeared in 2023, and rose from 1.7% that year to 18.8% in 2025. For dissertations filed during the first five months of 2026, 29.4% of abstracts contained AI-generated text. AI use was highest in mathematical and computer sciences: 36% of the abstracts had been written using AI. About 41% of dissertations by graduates educated in non-English-speaking countries had AI-generated abstracts, compared with 23% of dissertations by those from English-speaking countries.
Ang Liu, an engineer at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, says that one issue with PhD students using generative AI tools to write their dissertations is that researchers are expected to explore areas in which the answers are not already known. AI can be extremely helpful when students are working in areas in which there is already a substantial body of knowledge, he says. However, the challenge comes when research moves into areas in which knowledge is incomplete or uncertain. “That is where rigorous research training becomes even more important,” he says.
Job pathways
The researchers also reviewed PhD graduates’ education and employment profiles on the social-media platform LinkedIn. Among PhD graduates who completed their undergraduate degrees in the United States, those with AI-generated abstracts were 17% less likely to be employed in academia than were graduates who did not use AI. However, using AI made those graduates 16% more likely to be employed in industry than those who did not use it. The authors found that the link between AI use and landing a job in academia was less pronounced for graduates who did their undergraduate studies outside the US.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Starlink disruptions expose European reliance on US tech - Yahoo News UK
articles.summary: Ukraine’s Starlink disruptions expose European reliance on US tech  Yahoo News UK
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday that Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade satellite communications service, had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, which disrupted Ukrainian drones being used for attack missions and air defence.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also said Wednesday that for the second night in a row Ukraine had not received warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. The Space-Based Infrared System, a satellite constellation operated by the US military, provides early missile launch warnings.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear.
SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said Wednesday that any restrictions were Washington's responsibility. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military" and ultimately the president, Musk said.
Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukraine have soured after Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
European capacity limited
Ukraine's European allies have been unable to offer immediate alternatives, highlighting the reliance on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems..
European operator Eutelsat's OneWeb network offers satellite connectivity, but industry analysts say capacity and performance constraints make it unsuitable for frontline use. Switching networks would also mean swapping out thousands of Starlink terminals, as the two systems are not interconnected.
European Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius acknowledged the broader problem at a conference in Brussels on Wednesday.
Europe is "quite dependent on American space capabilities", he said, calling for the continent to develop its own systems.
He pointed to the European Union's IRIS² satellite constellation, a planned network of nearly 300 satellites that aims to rival Starlink and other US satellite internet service providers such as Amazon's Project Kuiper.
However, that project remains at least four years from becoming fully operational.
Germany is also developing a military satellite constellation, and Kubilius urged European countries to work together.

NVIDIA RTX Spark is a fresh new Windows PC platform. It was first announced at Computex 2026, and now, the first devices are finally hitting shelves. In our initial impressions, we called RTX Spark a Direct Shot at the PC Market, Backed by a Multi-Gen Roadmap That Past ‘Windows on Arm’ Bids Never Had.
The RTX Spark platform is very familiar for those who have used a DGX Spark system before.
But for the rest, while RTX Spark would be their first WoA (Windows on Arm) experience, there is little to no difference between using a standard x86 device and NVIDIA's RTX Spark thanks to software optimizations and fine-tuning of the Windows ecosystem around the RTX Spark. You'll be able to start right off the bat, and the best part is the whole experience is catered around NVIDIA's rich RTX and AI technologies, which PC users have become accustomed to over the many years.
So today, we get to share with you our first tests and initial impressions of a real NVIDIA RTX Spark product. What we'll be testing today is the ASUS ProArt P16, one of the many PCs that feature NVIDIA's latest N1X chip in its fullest configuration. The laptop was provided by NVIDIA during its RTX Spark Editor's Day event just a week ago, so while we may not be able to cover all tests in this review, we will be providing our readers with more performance benchmarks and updates as we spend more time with the device.
ASUS ProArt P16 "RTX Spark" Laptop - Specifications At A Glance
In terms of specifications, the ASUS ProArt P16 is equipped with the NVIDIA N1X SoC, which comes in two configurations. Our test unit featured the full die configuration of 20 CPU cores and a 6144 CUDA Core GPU. The N1X chip is based on TSMC's 3nm process across both dies (CPU/GPU).
The laptop was configured with the RTX Spark N1X chip, which features 20 cores & 20 threads. There are 10 "Arm Cortex-X925" performance-optimized cores and 10 "Arm Cortex-A725" cores optimized for efficiency. The performance cores feature a maximum boost clock of 4.0-4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores feature a maximum core clock of 2.8 GHz.
The chip features a total of 24 MB of L3 cache and 25 MB of L2 cache arranged in 20 MB (2 MB per core) for the Performance Core clusters and 5 MB (512KB per core) for the Efficiency Core cluster. The total onboard cache on the chip is 49 MB.
For the iGPU, NVIDIA is using its latest GB20B chip based on the Blackwell architecture, which features up to 6144 Cores across 48 SMs. It features 5th Gen Tensor Cores with DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, NVFP4 support, and RTX Ray Tracing cores. It produces up to 31 TFLOPs of FP32 and 1000 TOPS of NVFP4 (FP4) compute for AI workloads. The GPU also gets an additional 24 MB of L2 cache.

Moving into the memory system, the NVIDIA N1X SoC features support for 256b LPDDR5x (UMA) with up to 9400 MT/s speeds, enabling up to 300 GB/s of raw bandwidth, and up to 128 GB of maximum capacity. The system fabric is a high-performance coherent fabric that offers support for the CHI-E Coherency Protocol. The GPU has access to the entire system bandwidth of 600 GB/s (Aggregate) over the C2X interface.
The 128 GB Unified Memory pool is a significant step for NVIDIA in the PC segment. While its RTX and RTX PRO GPUs are potent solutions for gaming, content creation, and AI, the majority of these GPUs feature 8-32 GB of VRAM, while the fastest option, the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, carries 96GB of VRAM. Up to 128 GB of memory allows RTX Spark to handle larger render scenes and larger AI models, serving multiple agents.
There's also 16 MB of System Level Cache, which serves as L4 for the CPU, and enables power-efficient data-sharing between the multiple engines on the SoC. The C2C interface is also high-bandwidth and low-power, enabled through NVIDIA's NVLINK architecture.
On the connectivity side, NVIDIA's N1X SoC offers PCIe Gen5, four USB4 (40 Gbps per port) ports, DP 2.0 + HDMI 2.1a + 1 HDMI, and Wi-Fi7 support. Security features include Dual Secure Root support, SROOT processor, OSROOT processor, and support for both fTPM and discrete TPM. The whole chip has a TDP of 45-80W. NVIDIA claims that the laptop is able to sustain full performance even when running on battery, which is quite impressive.
Our review unit was equipped with a 2 TB PCIe Gen4 SSD. The laptop comes with two NVMe 2280 M.2 slots. It can be pre-configured with 16 TB of capacity.
IO includes three USB4 Type-C ports, a single USB 3.2 Gen2 Type-A port, a single 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack, a single HDMI 2.1 FRL display output, and an SD Express 7.0 card reader. It also comes with an FHD camera with IR functions, a backlit keyboard with chiclet design and 1.7mm key travel, a haptic touchpad with multi-gesture support, & WIFI7+BT5.4 capabilities.
The laptop comes in two 16" screen options: a UDH+ OLED (3840x2400 WQUXGA) panel with 700 nits of brightness (1600 HDR), a 120Hz refresh rate, and a 3K OLED panel (2880x1800) with 500 nits of brightness (1100 HDR), and up to a 120Hz refresh rate. There's a built-in array of microphones and speakers with Smart Amp technology.
The laptop is very compact and lightweight, featuring a 1.29-1.59 cm thin design and weighing roughly 1.77 kg or 3.90lbs. The battery is a 99.9 Wh 4S1P 4-Cell Li-ion design, which is charged by a 140W Type-C power adapter.
ASUS ProArt P16 Laptop - CPU Performance
We start by comparing the 3DMark CPU Profile tests. The RTX Spark lags behind x86 options with higher core/thread counts in multi-threading, and also in single-core tests.
The memory bandwidth on the RTX Spark is the fastest of the bunch thanks to the wide 256-bit interface and the use of 9600 MT/s LPDDR5X memory.
For Blender, the RTX Spark outperforms the Panther Lake chip but is slower than Ryzen AI MAX+ 300 SoCs. Blender does offer many DLSS technologies, which will provide better performance vs. the chips used for comparison here.
In CPU-Z, the RTX Spark offers the fastest single- and multi-core performance out of the bunch.
For Cinebench, we see strong single- and multi-core performance on the N1X chip, leading against AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, Snapdragon X2 Elite, and Intel's top Panther Lake SoC.
In Geekbench 6, the Arm SoCs perform quite well. The RTX Spark leads against the Intel Panther Lake, and AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 300 SoCs.
In Procyon Office, the RTX Spark offers decent performance, but Panther Lake and Ryzen AI MAX lead the charts.
WinRAR's compression tests showcase Gorgon Point-like performance, which should be enough.

articles.summary: ByteDance ASIC Deal: Nvidia Funds Chips US Export Controls Meant to Block  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
ByteDance is close to an agreement to buy custom AI chips from Taiwan's MediaTek for use in its data centers — and the deal's most striking dimension is not the chips themselves but who financed the infrastructure they run on. Nvidia, barred by US export rules from selling its most advanced accelerators directly to ByteDance inside China, invested $3.5 billion in MediaTek bonds in exchange for the Taiwanese chipmaker adopting Nvidia's NVLink Fusion interconnect platform as the design foundation for every custom chip it builds. If the ByteDance deal closes, the TikTok parent will run application-specific integrated circuits — ASICs — that plug directly into Nvidia's rack-scale architecture, powered by Nvidia's own interconnect standard, financed by Nvidia's own capital.
That outcome was not what the export control regime was designed to produce.
Why ByteDance Needs Alternative Chips
US restrictions on AI chip exports to China have tightened in multiple rounds since October 2022, when the Bureau of Industry and Security barred transfers of accelerators at or above the performance of Nvidia's A100. Subsequent rounds targeted high-bandwidth memory; a Trump administration freeze in April 2025 halted all China-bound AI chip shipments before partial loosening later that year allowed H200 GPU exports under specific conditions. ByteDance has publicly maintained that it follows all applicable US regulations. The company has been building a multi-vendor, multi-jurisdiction chip strategy to function across multiple regulatory scenarios rather than waiting for policy to stabilize.
ByteDance is weighing capital expenditure of as much as $70 billion in 2026 — more than double last year's total of roughly $25 billion — as it races to build out the data centers and computing capacity needed to power Doubao, its AI assistant, which had approximately 345 million monthly active users as of March 2026, and to compete with US AI leaders. The company plans to underwrite much of that spending through the roughly $50 billion in profit it generated in 2025. In September, ByteDance finalized a $29.6 billion syndicated loan to further fuel the buildout.
ByteDance also controls a significant share of China's total data-center capacity, a position it is aggressively working to expand.
What ASICs Are and Why ByteDance Wants Millions of Them
A general-purpose GPU — the kind Nvidia manufactures and that ByteDance cannot freely import — can train new AI models, run inference on existing ones, and be repurposed across changing architectures. That flexibility comes at a cost: a GPU optimized for everything is optimal for nothing in particular.
An ASIC takes the opposite approach. It is a chip designed from the ground up for one specific class of workload, built once and not reprogrammable afterward. For a company running a production AI chatbot at the scale of Doubao — where the workload is defined inference on a stable model architecture, not exploratory training — that tradeoff is favorable. The non-recurring engineering cost of designing a custom ASIC can run into the millions of dollars, but at ByteDance's volume, the efficiency gain per query makes the economics work. Independent analysis estimates well-designed AI inference ASICs can be three to ten times more energy-efficient than general-purpose GPUs running the same task.
Doubao processed more than 180 trillion tokens per day as of mid-2026, a volume that has grown roughly 1,500-fold in under two years. At that scale, even marginal per-query efficiency improvements translate into hundreds of millions of dollars in reduced infrastructure cost annually.
How the MediaTek Deal Fits ByteDance's Chip Playbook
The MediaTek arrangement is not ByteDance's first move away from Nvidia dependence — it is the latest layer in an already sprawling multi-vendor strategy.
In May 2026, ByteDance agreed to buy millions of ASICs from Qualcomm, which introduced its dedicated data-center brand, Dragonfly, at Computex 2026. That deal reportedly stays within US export-permitted compute thresholds, making it legally compliant — though it remains a strategic end-run around the spirit of a regime aimed at limiting China's AI chip access. In June, Reuters reported ByteDance was in talks to purchase at least 50,000 AI inference chips from Iluvatar CoreX, a Shanghai-based GPU startup that until recently sold almost entirely to government buyers. That deal would make ByteDance Iluvatar's first major commercial-scale customer and ByteDance's third domestic Chinese GPU supplier, alongside Huawei Ascend and Cambricon. ByteDance has also arranged access to Nvidia Blackwell GPU clusters through third-party cloud partners operating outside China, staying within the letter of US export regulations by keeping that hardware off Chinese soil.
If completed, the MediaTek agreement adds a qualitatively different dimension: custom, ASIC-level silicon designed specifically around ByteDance's platform and manufactured by a world-class Taiwanese foundry partner with established ties to both Google and Nvidia.
How NVLink Fusion Works — and What It Actually Costs ByteDance
This is where the architecture matters. NVLink Fusion, which Nvidia introduced in May 2025, is a chiplet-based technology that opens Nvidia's proprietary NVLink interconnect to third-party chip designers for the first time. Before Fusion, NVLink was exclusively Nvidia's — a proprietary high-speed fabric connecting only Nvidia GPUs. At its current specification, NVLink 5.0 on Blackwell-generation hardware runs at a total bidirectional bandwidth of 1.8 terabytes per second, more than ten times the throughput of a PCIe Gen 6 link.
What NVLink Fusion does is extend that fabric to custom ASICs through a chiplet that physically connects a non-Nvidia accelerator to the NVLink scale-up network. A MediaTek-built ASIC designed with NVLink Fusion integration can connect to Nvidia rack-scale systems — the MGX architecture, the NVSwitch fabric, the NVIDIA Rosa CPU interconnect — as if it were a first-party chip.
For ByteDance, this means faster chip-to-chip communication inside its data centers and a shorter time to deployment: a custom ASIC that already speaks NVLink does not need its own interconnect stack designed from scratch. For Nvidia, it means something more strategically significant. As analyst Matt Kimball of Moor Insights & Strategy has noted, hyperscalers designing "Nvidia-alternative" silicon now have three scale-up interconnect options: scale-up Ethernet, NVLink Fusion, and UALink — the open-standards alternative championed by AMD and Intel. Choosing NVLink Fusion, as MediaTek has, means ByteDance's custom ASICs cannot be migrated to AMD or Intel rack infrastructure without redesigning the interconnect layer.
Forbes and multiple technology analysts have called this Nvidia's chip tollbooth strategy: every company building an "Nvidia-alternative" accelerator through MediaTek's ASIC program is still buying Nvidia's connective tissue. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Charles Shum has warned that Nvidia's role as MediaTek's primary financial backer could weaken MediaTek's appeal to hyperscalers seeking genuine independence from Nvidia. ByteDance, for its part, appears to be accepting that tradeoff: the efficiency and supply-chain benefits of MediaTek's ASIC program outweigh the additional platform lock-in.
MediaTek's Pivot From Smartphones to Data Centers
For MediaTek, landing ByteDance would be the most significant validation of a strategic reinvention the company has been executing for several years.
Long known as the world's largest mobile SoC supplier by volume — powering budget and mid-range Android smartphones globally — MediaTek has been repositioning as a premium custom silicon provider for AI data centers. Its involvement in Google's TPU program established the initial proof point: the company designed Google Ironwood TPU modules, taking on input/output work for an inference-optimized accelerator, taking work that had been almost exclusively held by Broadcom. UBS estimated MediaTek stood to gain $4 billion from that collaboration. Google aims to produce approximately five million Ironwood TPU units in 2027 and scale to seven million in 2028, a volume trajectory that underpins much of MediaTek's revenue growth outlook.
MediaTek's AI and data-center chip revenue for 2026 is forecast at roughly $2 billion — approximately double its earlier estimate, reflecting accelerating demand. The company has set a 2027 target of capturing as much as 15% of an $80 billion custom AI ASIC market. Bernstein analysts project the global data-center XPU ASIC market could reach $250–$300 billion by 2028.
The Nvidia convertible bond deal, which saw Nvidia purchase $3.5 billion of bonds issued by MediaTek in one of the largest such issuances ever by a Taiwanese company, deepened the relationship materially. As part of the arrangement, MediaTek committed to making NVLink Fusion the design foundation for the custom AI accelerators it builds for hyperscaler clients. MediaTek's shares climbed in Taipei trading on Thursday after the Bloomberg report of the ByteDance talks emerged.
What Comes Next for Competitors
The reported deal has already unsettled competitive positioning. Qualcomm and Broadcom — both of which compete for custom ASIC contracts from hyperscalers — face a more crowded field if MediaTek establishes ByteDance as a second major reference customer alongside Google. Broadcom, Google's primary TPU co-designer for years, is now sharing that role with MediaTek. Adding ByteDance as a second large customer would give MediaTek a second platform to demonstrate data-center capabilities at scale.
Nvidia's position is, by design, more protected than it might initially appear. Losing direct GPU sales to ByteDance in China has already been priced into its business by export control realities. The NVLink Fusion strategy means the ByteDance-MediaTek deal reduces ByteDance's reliance on Nvidia

articles.title: What Is Starshield, SpaceX's Military Version of Starlink, and Why Is It So Important to Ukraine? - Time Magazine
articles.summary: What Is Starshield, SpaceX's Military Version of Starlink, and Why Is It So Important to Ukraine?  Time Magazine
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian forces said Wednesday its battlefield efforts had been hampered overnight after losing some access to SpaceX’s military-grade satellite Internet service, which has become a lifeline as Kyiv weathers Moscow's attacks.
Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has recently been used by Ukrainian forces to strengthen its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military technology expert who advises Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, said speed restrictions had been imposed on the "military package" of Starshield services, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. “Our defense forces have not received any warnings about this restriction,” he said. Beskrestnov claimed the restrictions, which he said applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were “related to the current political situation.” He did not offer further details.
Tensions are high between the U.S. and Ukraine, as Zelensky has been vocal in his disapproval of U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import diesel from Russia, despite previous sanctions prohibiting it. The move has also caused a split in Trump’s own party, with several Republican lawmakers urging him to reverse course. After making the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine—but Zelensky swiftly accused Moscow of violating any such agreement and Ukraine has, in turn, resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries, despite pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace" in an interview that aired Thursday.
Speaking from the U.K., Zelensky said Wednesday it was a “pity” Ukrainian forces had experienced “difficulties” with Starlink services and intelligence, adding that he was surprised by the developments in Ukraine’s partnership with the U.S. In an interview on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Zelensky suggested he believed Starlink had been slowed down to damage him, and warned “people will die, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful.” He said he hoped the restriction was only a “mistake,” suggesting it was perhaps "a huge technical problem” at SpaceX.
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk addressed the matter, insisting that Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.”
Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, later reported that the decision came from inside the White House.
TIME has reached out to the White House for further comment.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian national news agency Ukrinform reported Thursday, citing sources within the Ministry of Defense, that the Starshield service had resumed. TIME has reached out to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense for comment.
The discourse has raised questions about what Starshield is and how uniquely important it has become on the Ukrainian battlefield.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a program developed by Musk’s SpaceX that draws on the satellite and launch capability behind Starlink, its commercial satellite Internet network, to support national security operations.
“Starlink is basic interconnectivity, it's like the Internet. Starshield essentially grows out of the experience of Starlink,” Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King’s College London, tells TIME.
But the military value of that connectivity extends far beyond access to the Internet, Hilborne adds.
“In and of itself, satellite communications are not military technology, but it enables the military to communicate and amass a real-time, multi-domain picture of the battlefield, which some argue nobody else actually has at this stage,” he says.
Both systems also offer high-speed connectivity because of the satellite technology underpinning them.
“Starlink and Starshield are low on the Earth’s orbit, and they have a very high bandwidth, so lots of information can pass through those satellites, with virtually no delay on the signal,” Hilborne says.
There are more than 10,000 satellites in the Starlink network, while Hilborne says Starshield uses “a much smaller number of satellites.” However, the exact number of satellites associated with Starshield remains unknown, with experts telling TIME that such details are closely guarded due to national security considerations.
“They keep the contracting details on these things classified,” says Todd Harrison, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.
SpaceX, on its website, says Starshield is “designed to support U.S. National Defense use cases for the Department of Defense and other government partners.”
How is Starshield different from Starlink?
While both systems rely on closely related satellite technology, they differ in the services they provide and how they are intended to be used.
“Starshield refers to military services that actually operate through Starlink,” Harrison explains, comparing the services to “two different brands of a cell phone provider, even though your phone calls are going through the same towers.”
Starshield offers additional capabilities designed for military operations, including more advanced encryption and satellite imaging, experts tell TIME.
“It's got another extra set of capabilities over and above Starlink,” Hilborne says. “They use some of the same technologies, but it would be highly encrypted, and they have different sensors that allow them to image what they call ‘Earth observation.’ That can give a radar imaging of the Earth [which] has advantages over optical pictures.”
Yet experts say the distinction between the two systems is not always clear, particularly given how closely their underlying technology and operations are connected.
How important is Starshield for Ukraine?
Starshield and the satellite communications technology underpinning it have become vital to Ukraine’s military operations against Russia.
Hilborne describes the technology as “highly critical” to Ukraine, explaining that any restrictions could cut communications with military equipment traveling above that speed, leaving operators without the information needed to guide their missions, as once that speed threshold is exceeded, the connection “suddenly cuts off and it's flying blind,” he says.
The consequences are particularly serious for Ukrainian drone operations, which rely on communications for both strikes against Russian targets and defensive missions against incoming attacks.
“It's really critical for drones, both the offensive medium range strikes, but also affects Ukraine's ability to fly defensive drones against the incoming Russian drones,” says Hilborne.
Beyond its role in drone missions, experts say satellite communications also offer important advantages over other forms of battlefield connectivity.
Harrison notes that “the big benefit of using satellite-based communications is that you can communicate over longer distances in a variety of terrain, and it does have some jam-resistant features to overcome electronic forms of attack.”
