articles.title: Musk calls for Zelenskyy to quit as Starlink row strains US-Ukraine ties - The Federal
articles.summary: Musk calls for Zelenskyy to quit as Starlink row strains US-Ukraine ties  The Federal
articles.full_text:
Ukraine’s reliance on US-controlled satellite communications has come under scrutiny after disruptions to Starlink and Starshield, intensifying calls for Kyiv and Europe to build independent defence capabilities
Amid a verbal war with Mukesh Ambani over the delay in India allowing his satellite-based internet service Starlink to operate in the country, tech billionaire Elon Musk on Wednesday (October 14) called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to step down, as tensions mounted between Kyiv and Washington over US support for Ukraine’s war against Russia.
“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote on X. “Time for Zelenskyy to go.”
The remarks followed Ukraine’s call for Musk to restore Starlink, the satellite internet system developed by his SpaceX company, which Kyiv says has been slowed down. Ukraine has accused the United States of indirectly helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and limiting its military response through changes to the satellite system.
This brings into focus India’s regulatory bodies dragging their feet in giving Starlink access to the Indian market and reports about Jio Platforms gaining approval from India’s space regulator to launch satellite internet in the country.
Growing friction
The dispute comes amid growing friction between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy recently answered in the affirmative when asked whether he felt “betrayed” after Trump announced a diesel-supply deal with heavily-sanctioned Russia.
Facing crucial midterm elections next month, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for tightening fuel supplies and driving up prices at the pump.
Also Read: Ukraine ready to consider India's ceasefire proposal: FM Sybiha
Musk blamed the US government for any disruption, distinguishing between Starshield, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications and which he said was controlled by Washington, and Starlink, the civilian satellite network that Ukraine also uses but is not permitted to deploy for offensive operations.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X.
What is Starshield?
SpaceX publicly announced Starshield in late 2022 as a secure satellite network designed for government customers and national security operations.
Unlike Starlink, which provides internet connectivity to households, businesses, and other users, Starshield is designed to support classified communications and US national defence requirements. Its customers include the US Department of Defense and other government agencies.
Also Read: Centre rejects Elon Musk’s Starlink ‘Oligarchs’ allegation, says rules are fair
The US government has invested billions of dollars in the technology, while the Pentagon has enabled Ukraine to use the service.
How does it work?
Starshield and Starlink rely on the same basic satellite technology. SpaceX has deployed thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit, creating a network capable of providing internet connectivity to terminals on the ground.
These terminals can be installed on vehicles and other platforms, including drones, allowing them to receive satellite internet and maintain communications during operations. However, Starshield incorporates additional security features intended for sensitive government and military applications.
Also Read: Musk takes fresh swipe at Ambani, says Starlink will benefit Indian consumers
Musk has described Starlink as a civilian service and Starshield as its military counterpart. In 2023, he said Starshield would be owned by the US government and controlled by the US Space Force.
Nevertheless, questions remain about how distinct the two services are, particularly because outages have affected both. Ukraine has also relied on Starlink for military communications despite its civilian designation.
No easy European alternative
The disruption has underscored Ukraine’s dependence on American technology for battlefield communications and missile detection, despite strong support for Kyiv from European countries.
The US Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellite constellation provides early warnings of missile launches by detecting the heat generated during launch.
Europe lacks a ready-made alternative to Starlink that Ukrainian soldiers can readily attach to drones. European governments and companies are exploring alternatives, but significant technological and operational hurdles remain.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat surged on Wednesday as investors anticipated that growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv could boost demand for European satellite services.
Also Read: Five ways the Russia-Ukraine war has changed the world forever
However, independent satellite consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp told Reuters that Eutelsat’s OneWeb network was not well suited to frontline military operations. He cited limitations in capacity and performance, as well as the cost, weight, bulk, and power consumption of user terminals.
Eutelsat said it continued to provide connectivity services in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit networks with partners, but declined further comment because of the sensitive nature of the situation.
Von der Ropp added that switching networks would require replacing thousands of terminals because Starlink and Starshield equipment uses proprietary technology and cannot simply connect to OneWeb.
Push for strategic autonomy
The disruption has intensified calls for Ukraine and Europe to reduce their reliance on a single provider for critical defence communications.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defence technology startup Buntar Aerospace, told Reuters that the incident demonstrated the risks of depending exclusively on one system.
Also Read: Russia snubs Ukraine's unilateral ceasefire, firing dozens of drones
“You can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off,” he said, adding that countries needed sovereign capabilities to avoid being “subject to somebody’s mood today”.
European concerns about dependence on American defence technology have grown as Trump has threatened to withdraw from NATO, while European leaders regard Russia as the continent’s biggest security threat in decades.

Breaking News
Ukraine says US Starlink restrictions are disrupting its drones as Russia launches new attacks.
On October 14, 2026, SpaceX enforced a 100 mph (161 km/h) velocity cap on Starshield and Starlink military satellite terminals used by Ukraine, severing live communication links for long-range unmanned aerial systems and aerial interceptors. The restriction degrades real-time command, control, and targeting relays for fixed-wing drones operating behind front lines and limits pursuit capabilities against Russian Shahed loitering munitions. Ground-speed enforcement prevents satellite antenna handovers at higher velocities, disrupting flight guidance without physically altering the drone's mechanical engine performance.
Starlink and Starshield terminals allow Ukrainian drones to transmit live video, receive targeting updates, and remain under operator control hundreds of kilometres beyond conventional radio range, enabling long-range strikes, reconnaissance, and interceptions against Russian forces. (Picture source: Ukrainian MoD)
On October 14, 2026, Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov announced that SpaceX imposed a 100 mph (161 km/h) speed limit on Starlink military satellite terminals used by Ukrainian forces, disrupting middle-strike drones, aerial interceptors, reconnaissance flights, and communications relays amid renewed Russian missile and Shahed attacks. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov confirmed that the Starshield restriction arrived without warning, while Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps had to cancel several drone missions in the Huliaipole sector of Zaporizhzhia Oblast after losing connectivity. Serhii Sternenko suspected that Washington had requested the change amid U.S. President Donald Trump's pressure on Kyiv to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and threats to reduce intelligence sharing, although no American order was confirmed.
Elon Musk responded that Starshield was controlled by the U.S. government, with usage restrictions determined by the U.S. military and ultimately the president. Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed that connectivity had stabilized at speeds up to 160 km/h by October 14 evening, but negotiations with SpaceX and American authorities to remove the restriction continued. The 161 km/h ceiling applies to the ground speed of the terminal carrying the satellite antenna, not the drone's mechanical performance or internet bandwidth. At 160 km/h, a drone travels 44.4 m/s, compared with 55.6 m/s at 200 km/h and 69.4 m/s at 250 km/h. However, a drone maintaining an airspeed of 150 km/h with a 20 km/h tailwind would reach 170 km/h, exceeding the terminal limit. In Ukraine, commercial Starlink terminals already faced movement restrictions of 75–90 km/, partly to prevent Russian use aboard attack drones.
Related topic: Ukraine's new AI-powered drone campaign across Crimea could collapse Russia's Southern Front
On October 14, however, Ukrainian units experienced connectivity losses between 72 and 161 km/h, indicating that the initial service degradation extended below the nominal ceiling in several cases. The Starlink restriction therefore does not stop a Ukrainian drone from flying faster, but can sever the communications connection carrying vital flight commands, live video, and targeting information. Ukraine's current middle-strike drone campaign covers Russian ammunition depots, fuel convoys, vehicle concentrations, and logistics routes located 50 to 200 km behind the front line, particularly in occupied Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrainian units increasingly fitted these drones with Starlink terminals during 2026, enabling attacks beyond the effective coverage of conventional ground-based radio-control links.
At 250 km/h, a Ukrainian drone reaches Russian targets 50, 100, and 200 km away in 12, 24, and 48 minutes, respectively; at 160 km/h, those times increase to 18 minutes 45 seconds, 37 minutes 30 seconds, and 75 minutes. For a 150 km outbound mission, the restriction consequently requires 56 minutes 15 seconds instead of 36 minutes, increasing outbound flight time by 56.25%, excluding loitering and terminal manoeuvres. Longer transit times can reduce the usefulness of targeting information against moving convoys, increase exposure to Russian electronic warfare and air defense, and alter the fuel reserves available for manoeuvring near the target. The restriction is particularly consequential for fixed-wing drones whose minimum sustainable airspeed, combined with wind conditions, prevents them from remaining below the terminal's permitted ground speed, unless they find alternative communications.
Starlink connects Ukrainian drones through low-Earth-orbit satellites using Ku- and Ka-band frequencies, electronically steered antennas, and satellite handovers, reducing dependence on terrestrial radio stations. Under a simplified geometric line-of-sight calculation, a drone flying at 100 metres altitude with a ground antenna 2 metres high has a radio horizon of 55.4 km, increasing to 92.7 km at 500 metres altitude. Terrain, electronic warfare, and antenna performance can further constrain practical communications distances, explaining the use of satellite terminals for missions extending 100 to 200 km behind Russian positions. Some drones carry Starshield directly, while others relay commands and video between additional drones and ground operators.
If a satellite-equipped relay loses connectivity above 161 km/h, several dependent drones can lose their communications path simultaneously. Replacing that connection requires additional airborne relays, elevated antennas, or ground stations, and the resulting network must maintain coverage along the entire drone's route rather than only at its launch point. The restriction also affects Ukraine's interception of Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, capable of speeds approaching 322 km/h, equivalent to 89.4 m/s. At that speed, a Ukrainian interceptor maintaining the Starlink limit of 160 km/h travels 44.4 m/s, leaving a 45 m/s disadvantage during pursuit from behind. Consequently, a Russian drone initially 5 km ahead would increase that separation by 2.7 km every minute if both maintained those speeds, meaning the interceptor cannot neutralize the threat.
In a head-on engagement, the combined closing speed reaches 482 km/h, equivalent to 133.9 m/s, reducing the time available for terminal guidance and target identification. Ukrainian interceptors can physically exceed the Starshield ceiling, but risk losing operator commands and video reception unless alternative radio control or autonomous terminal guidance is available. The number of missed interceptions attributable to the October 14 disruption remains unquantified, but it occurred during successive Russian attacks against Kyiv, Kropyvnytskyi, Dnipro, and energy infrastructure. Ukraine began using Starlink after Russia's February 24, 2022 invasion and the simultaneous cyberattack against Viasat satellite communications. Mykhailo Fedorov requested SpaceX assistance on February 26, and the first terminals arrived on February 28.
By March, Ukrainian command centers and special operations units were using the service, followed by defenders of Mariupol and Azovstal during the Russian siege in April and May 2022. Artillery formations subsequently integrated this satellite connectivity into target exchange and fire correction, while applications expanded during 2023 and 2024 to reconnaissance drones, infantry communications, mobile command posts, and unmanned naval vessels operating in the Black Sea. Notably, SpaceX had already restricted certain Ukrainian offensive drone applications in February 2023, distinguishing military communications from direct weapons employment. The October 2026 measure therefore affected an established military communication network, with the greatest immediate consequences for unmanned aircraft requiring continuous satellite links while travelling above the authorized speed, either to strike or defend.
SpaceX's relationship with the U.S. government includes a $150 million Space Development Agency contract in October 2020 for four missile-tracking satellites launched in April 2023. Elon Musk then introduced Starshield, the military variant of Starlink, in December 2022, and secured a U.S. Space Force communications contract in September 2023, expanding military access to commercial satellites. In February 2026, Ukraine and SpaceX cooperated to restrict unauthorized Russian Starlink terminals, reducing Moscow's ability to operate satellite-connected drones. Ukrainian forces subsequently expanded their Starlink use during middle-strike missions against Russian logistics within occupied territory.
On July 28, Zelensky sought American approval to employ these drones inside Russia, including potential attacks against mobile Iskander ballistic missile launchers used against Ukrainian civilians, but authorization remained unresolved by August 31. Musk opposed extending offensive Starlink operations into Russia, while maintaining on October 14 that Starshield usage restrictions were determined by American military authorities, including the U.S. President Donald Trump, but did not identify the official responsible for introducing the ceiling or establish whether it originated from a military requirement, a contractual limitation, or a political decision. However, and significantly, the Starlink restriction followed several days of deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks against Russian oil refineries, as President Trump threatened to withhold intelligence sharing and military assistance unless Ukraine stopped.
Kyiv initially agreed to pause refinery strikes for three days even as Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian electricity infrastructure, as Trump sought to promote an energy ceasefire that Moscow refused to accept. On October 12, five Russian S-400 ballistic missiles struck Kyiv s

articles.full_text:
The US space industry is entering a phase of mass production, which is changing the industrial real estate market. Companies that until recently were mainly looking for labs and engineering teams are now leasing factories, building production campuses and reserving space years before they are ready.
In the first half of the year, space companies attracted $11.3 billion in venture capital. Among them are Varda Space Industries, Sierra Space and Astranis. 78% of the global space economy is private, according to the Space Foundation, and private investment in the sector is expected to reach a record $100 billion this year.
“There is no other industry where real estate is such a powerful catalyst for a company’s future success,“ said Mac Burridge, managing director of advanced manufacturing at JLL in Los Angeles.
Former toy factory to build spacecraft
One of the most telling examples is the deal by Varda Space Industries in El Segundo, California. In March, the company leased a 205,000-square-foot former Mattel factory. The building, which used to make Hot Wheels and Barbie, will be used to build spacecraft.
Varda is developing automated laboratories and satellite platforms that are launched into orbit. In microgravity, the labs grow molecular crystals for the pharmaceutical industry. This is the company's second facility in El Segundo, part of the South Bay area of Los Angeles.
The area attracts aerospace and defense companies because of its talent pool and the presence of established aerospace companies. According to Burridge, Southern California is as important to these companies as the San Francisco area is to technology companies.
Land and power shortages slow new deals
Competition for industrial real estate in the South Bay is intensifying. About a third of industrial leases in the Los Angeles area in the third quarter were signed there. Net take-up is projected to reach 2.5 million square feet in 2026, about half of the region’s total.

Burridge reports demand for 5 million square feet of modern manufacturing space, with some tenants signing contracts 12 months in advance.
The problem isn’t just a lack of available buildings. New manufacturing sites need more electrical capacity, and securing the necessary connections in the South Bay can take up to 24 months.
„There are no existing buildings left to accommodate them. “They’ve swallowed everything,” says Martin Pupil, partner and managing director at Stream Realty Partners.
New Campuses Near Spaceports
The growth is also being felt outside of California. In Brevard County, Florida, Hines has broken ground on the second phase of the Space Coast Innovation Hub on a 100-acre site. The project will add 1.1 million square feet of manufacturing and logistics space near Cape Canaveral.
Also in the works in the area are the 307,000-square-foot NASA Causeway Logistics Center, Amazon’s 24-acre Project Satellite in Titusville, and Blue Origin’s 830,000-square-foot manufacturing facility.
In early October, Blue Origin announced a satellite manufacturing campus in Hutto, Texas. The investment is $550 million, the area is 1.3 million square feet, and the promised new jobs are 2,000.
Companies choose locations based on the availability of staff, vacant land and electrical capacity. Local governments compete for projects with financial incentives. A speed limit from space, and drones go down at the front: SpaceX has restricted Starlink connections for Ukraine’s military without warning. The restrictions affect Starshield terminals, the military version of Starlink, which are mounted on drones and vehicles. According to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, they now work reliably only at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour), Reuters reported. Several missions had to be called off.
What Is Happening at the Front
The Starshield terminals are central to Ukraine’s war effort: They are used to steer drones in real time, for example in strikes on Russian supply lines or to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones. According to one Ukrainian military unit, connections dropped out for 10 to 20 seconds at speeds of just 110 to 120 kilometers per hour. The drones kept flying but became very hard to control. The activist Serhii Sternenko, citing military sources, even reported outages at 60 to 70 kilometers per hour.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, the connection stabilized over the course of the day, but the 160-kilometer-per-hour cap remains in place. The ministry says it is negotiating with SpaceX to prevent such sudden restrictions in the future.
‘This Cannot Be a Coincidence’
Officials in Kyiv do not believe it was a technical problem. The move “cannot be a coincidence,” Mr. Beskrestnov told The Kyiv Independent, pointing to the political situation. President Trump had previously declared an “energy cease-fire” and pressed Ukraine to stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries. He reportedly threatened to withhold intelligence. There is no evidence of a link to the Starlink throttling, however, and the White House has not commented.
Sharp criticism also came from Poland. Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asked Elon Musk on X whether he was playing politics with his products again. Poland funds Ukraine’s use of Starlink with about $50 million (roughly €45 million) a year, according to earlier statements by Mr. Sikorski.
The Counterpoint: Musk Points to the U.S. Military
Mr. Musk has rejected responsibility. Restrictions on the speed or use of Starshield terminals are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately the president, he said. Starlink may also be used only for civilian or defensive purposes, not for offensive military operations, according to Mr. Musk. SpaceX has not yet given an official explanation.
Europe’s Dependence on Musk
The incident shows once again how dependent Ukraine, and with it Europe, is on the infrastructure of a single American entrepreneur. There are hardly any real alternatives so far. Eutelsat operates its own satellite network in low Earth orbit with OneWeb, but it has far fewer satellites in space. The E.U.’s planned IRIS² satellite network is not expected to be operational until the end of the decade. That is why Ukraine is also working on its own solutions: The Ukrainian defense tech company Stetman is developing UASAT-NANO, an independent satellite communications system. Meanwhile, European space start-ups such as Isar Aerospace are building their own launch vehicles so that satellites can reach orbit without relying on SpaceX.

The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” Elon Musk via X
What is starlink?
Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is the main profit engine of SpaceX.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Watch more Starlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain's defence ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

Taiwan's Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin said the proposed complex would help smaller suppliers that are essential to Nvidia's production ecosystem establish operations in the U.S.
That includes companies supporting TSMC as well as AI server assemblers such as Foxconn.
The Texas project is part of a broader effort to build a more complete AI and semiconductor supply chain in the U.S. rather than relying as heavily on components and manufacturing concentrated in Asia.
At the same time, Taiwan is moving in the opposite direction with China.
Taipei reportedly plans to tighten export restrictions on AI servers and advanced semiconductors, aligning more closely with U.S. controls designed to limit the flow of cutting-edge AI hardware into China.

Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, Kung said.

I think the bigger story is that Nvidia's supply chain is becoming increasingly Americanized on one side and restricted from China on the other.

articles.title: Starshield Ukraine: Who Controls Musk’s Satellites Under International Law? - Diplomacy and Law
articles.summary: Starshield Ukraine: Who Controls Musk’s Satellites Under International Law?  Diplomacy and Law

The Starshield Ukraine controversy emerged in October 2026 after restrictions on military satellite communications disrupted Ukrainian drone operations and raised questions about who controlled access to the service. On October 15, Reuters reported that instructions to restrict Starshield had originated inside the White House and were communicated to Defense Department leadership. The account relied on two anonymous U.S. officials and a Western official familiar with the matter. None identified the individual responsible for the decision (Banco and Slattery, 2026).
Ukrainian commanders reported interrupted missions and lost drones after connectivity deteriorated on fast-moving military platforms. Some units regained normal service by October 15, although the restrictions did not affect the entire Starlink network (Kullab, 2026). Elon Musk maintained that Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the U.S. government, with decisions about their use resting with American military authorities and ultimately the president. A senior U.S. official denied that President Donald Trump had personally requested the restriction (Banco and Slattery, 2026).
Starshield is operated by SpaceX and designed for government and national-security applications, using technology and infrastructure developed for its broader Starlink network (SpaceX, 2026). The distinction between operating a satellite system and controlling its military use is central to the dispute. Ownership of particular spacecraft, technical authority over service configurations, and the power to order operational restrictions may rest with different actors. The contractual arrangements governing the affected Ukrainian services have not been sufficiently disclosed to establish precisely how those responsibilities were allocated.
Under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, states bear international responsibility for their national activities in outer space, including those undertaken by nongovernmental entities. The provision also requires authorization and continuing supervision of such activities by the appropriate state party (United Nations, 1967). These obligations establish a specific regime for national space activities, but their application to restrictions implemented through terrestrial communications infrastructure requires careful legal assessment. Article VI does not itself guarantee Ukraine uninterrupted access to military satellite services.
A separate question is whether the restrictions constituted an internationally wrongful act. Under the general principles reflected in the International Law Commission's Articles on State Responsibility, such an act requires conduct attributable to a state and a breach of an international obligation, subject to any applicable special rules (ILC, 2001, Articles 2 and 55). The 2024 U.S.–Ukraine Bilateral Security Agreement provides a further context for defense cooperation, although its annex expressly excludes the creation of legal rights or obligations. Establishing who authorized the Starshield restrictions is consequently only part of determining their legal significance. The reported disruption does not, by itself, establish that the United States violated international law.
1. Starshield Ukraine: The October 2026 Restrictions
On October 14, 2026, Ukrainian military officials reported unexpected restrictions on satellite communications used to operate drones over Ukrainian territory. The disruption affected military-grade services associated with SpaceX’s Starshield system, particularly terminals installed aboard fast-moving aircraft. Ukrainian forces said the restrictions had been introduced without advance warning, forcing units to cancel missions and complicating operations against Russian forces in occupied territory (Dysa, 2026).
Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on military technology, reported that the affected service had stopped functioning at speeds above approximately 160 kilometers per hour, or 100 miles per hour. The Ukrainian 7th Rapid Reaction Corps separately described connection losses lasting between 10 and 20 seconds during flights at 110–120 kilometers per hour. Those interruptions occurred below the reported speed threshold and made drones more difficult to control. The observations established the operational problem without revealing the precise technical mechanism responsible (Dysa, 2026).
The restrictions affected particular military communications services, not the entire Starlink constellation. Ukrainian forces continued using satellite connectivity for other purposes, and the available reporting did not establish a nationwide interruption affecting civilian subscribers. By October 15, some military units reported that their connections had returned to the required operating speeds. The extent to which restrictions remained elsewhere was less certain (Kullab, 2026).
1.1 Who Ordered the Starshield Restrictions?
The controversy initially centered on SpaceX and Elon Musk, whose company develops the satellite technology used by Ukrainian forces. On October 14, Musk stated publicly that Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the United States government. According to his account, decisions concerning restrictions on speed or permitted use belonged to American military authorities and ultimately the president. The statement challenged the assumption that he had independently ordered the interruption (Dysa, 2026).
Reuters subsequently reported that the instruction originated inside the White House. Its October 15 investigation cited two American officials and a Western official familiar with the matter, who said Defense Department leadership had received a message directing that Starshield service for Ukrainian military operations be slowed. The officials spoke anonymously and did not identify who authorized the decision or who was responsible for implementing it (Banco and Slattery, 2026).
The White House's reported involvement does not establish that President Donald Trump personally issued the instruction. A senior American official denied that Trump had requested the restriction, while the administration did not clarify whether another official had done so. Ukrainian officials separately reported being informed that the decision came from the White House. These accounts support governmental involvement more strongly than the suggestion of an independently authorized decision by Musk, although the precise chain of command remains unresolved.
The Pentagon's role also requires careful distinction. Receiving an instruction does not necessarily mean that military personnel directly modified satellite service configurations. Implementation could have involved government officials, SpaceX personnel, or procedures established under defense contracts. The available reports establish neither the complete implementation process nor the individual responsible for applying the restrictions.
1.2 Military Consequences and the U.S.–Ukraine Dispute
Satellite communications have become important to Ukrainian drone operations because certain aircraft depend on external connections for guidance, video transmission, and communication with ground operators. Interruptions can prevent operators from maintaining effective control or receiving information needed to complete a mission. The consequences depend on the aircraft's technical capabilities and the duration of the communication loss.
Yevhen Karas, commander of Ukraine's 413th Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment, told the Associated Press that his unit experienced disruptions lasting approximately one day. He reported unsuccessful missions and the loss of drones after communications were interrupted. By October 15, connectivity had returned to the required speed for his unit, although Karas said he did not know whether the original interruption had been caused by a technical malfunction or a deliberate restriction (Kullab, 2026).
Other Ukrainian accounts described difficulties affecting strike operations against Russian positions and logistics in occupied territory. Reuters also reported that restrictions complicated the operation of interceptor drones used against incoming Russian drones. The consequences thus extended to offensive and defensive operations, although the available evidence does not establish how many aircraft or missions were affected across the Ukrainian armed forces (Banco and Slattery, 2026).
The disruption occurred amid serious disagreements between Washington and Kyiv. Reuters reported that American representatives expressed frustration with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries during an October 9 meeting in Miami. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff reportedly participated in conveying the administration's objections. The meeting formed part of a broader diplomatic dispute concerning Ukraine's attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and American efforts to influence the course of the war (Banco and Slattery, 2026).
The proximity of these events raises the possibility that the restrictions were intended to exert political pressure. Their timing, however, does not establish that motive. Reuters also reported that Ukrainian drones attacking refineries inside Russia relied on communications methods other than Starlink because the service was unavailable there. Restrictions affecting drones operating over Ukraine could disrupt military operations without directly disabling the refinery attacks that Washington opposed (Dysa, 2026).
2. Starshield vs. Starlink: Who Controls the Satellites?
Starlink and Starshield are related satellite systems developed by SpaceX, but their purposes and customer arrangements differ. Google's quantum lab just cleared a barrier that has quietly set the ceiling on how powerful a quantum computer can ever get, and the implications reach well beyond a single research paper.
Google Quantum AI published “Magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor” in the journal Science on October 15, 2026. The paper is the first hardware demonstration of a technique that cut errors 40-fold compared with states prepared without it.
Class A shares of Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG | GOOG Price Prediction, NASDAQ:GOOGL) rose 0.45% that day to close at $349.22, which valued the company at $4.27 trillion. A lab result like this changes very little. It strengthens a long-term research effort that Alphabet can fund with its own profits.
What Google Demonstrated on Willow
The experiment ran on Google’s Willow processor. It produced T-states, a type of magic state, at 99.99% logical fidelity, which means an error rate of 0.0001 or less.
Google researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones developed the method in 2024. It places an imperfect state in a small chip region. It checks the state with measurements, discards failures, and extends the survivors into a larger error-correcting code.
Only 8% of attempts passed the filter. Throwing away most attempts is how the method works, because it gives up volume to get quality.
Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai reacted on X that day. He wrote: “Some magical progress towards “magic state” in quantum!”

Complex quantum calculations need magic states. Each one can be used only once, so the machine has to keep making new ones. Some estimates say up to 95% of a quantum computer’s capacity could go to producing them.
Without a cheap, reliable supply of magic states, a quantum computer can only run calculations an ordinary computer already handles, and making them more cheaply reduces how large a machine you would need to build.

Google Quantum AI said it has demonstrated "magic state cultivation," which could be a practical solution to one of quantum computing's most severe bottlenecks.
Quick Take
- Google Quantum AI demonstrated “magic state cultivation” on its Willow processor, reducing errors 40-fold compared with uncultivated states and achieving 99.99% logical fidelity for T-states.
- Castle Island Ventures co-founder Nic Carter said AI-assisted advances are accelerating quantum computing progress, although no threat is imminent.
Google Quantum AI announced Thursday that it has experimentally shown that "magic state cultivation" works on its Willow processor, demonstrating what could be a practical solution to one of quantum computing's most severe bottlenecks.
So-called "magic states" are special quantum states used to enable operations needed for universal quantum computing. Producing high-quality, error-corrected versions of them has long been recognized as a major bottleneck by researchers, as some estimates indicated that up to 95% of a machine’s capacity could be consumed by making them.
In 2024, Google researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones started developing magic state cultivation as an approach that promises a significant reduction by adding what would act like a filter.
"You would inject a noisy state into a small region on a quantum chip, and then run a series of highly coordinated measurements to check for errors and remove any flawed attempts," Google explained. "[The] team showed how that would let you grow, or 'cultivate,' an exceptionally pure, low-error quantum state that you could simultaneously adapt into a larger, useful encoding."
Following a series of technical innovations and engineering, magic state cultivation on Google Quantum AI's Willow processor achieved a 40-fold reduction in errors and T-states with a record logical fidelity of 99.99%.
Google researchers noted that larger-scale demonstrations remain necessary before the approach can support practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Implications for crypto
Meanwhile, the crypto industry has been working to develop and adopt post-quantum cryptographic protections designed to resist attacks from large-scale quantum computers. Theoretically, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could break the digital signature schemes used to authorize cryptocurrency transactions, as well as public-key cryptographic systems across the broader internet and financial infrastructure.

TradingKey - Airbus, Italy's Leonardo, and France's Thales are advancing a space business consolidation plan codenamed "Project Bromo".
The three companies signed a memorandum of understanding on October 23, 2025, proposing to combine parts of their respective space operations into a new company. The project remains subject to final agreements, equity and operational arrangements, and an EU competition review, and has not yet been officially established.
Bromo is a proposed aerospace business consolidation plan spearheaded by Airbus, Leonardo, and Thales, covering satellite manufacturing, space systems, satellite communications, and related services.
Bloomberg previously reported that the joint venture's annual revenue could reach approximately 6.5 billion euros, with a preliminary equity structure of 35% held by Airbus and 32.5% each by Leonardo and Thales. These figures represent a preliminary proposal, and the final assets included, equity structure, and governance arrangements remain subject to adjustment.
According to a Bloomberg report on October 15, the EU is communicating with the three companies to accelerate the subsequent antitrust review process. Over the past year, discussions have primarily focused on potential competition concerns, and the companies are expected to submit a formal application in the coming weeks.
Europe is driving Bromo primarily to scale up its space industry and enhance local supply chains and key technological capabilities. SpaceX (SPCX) has established strong comprehensive capabilities in rocket launching, satellite manufacturing, and low-Earth orbit satellite communications, whereas European companies remain relatively fragmented, facing pressure in R&D investment, product iteration, and satellite deployment efficiency.
The EU is advancing its IRIS² secure satellite communications program, which could bring orders for government communications, defense space, and critical infrastructure to European companies in the future. However, such projects represent potential sources of demand and cannot be directly viewed as contracts already secured by Bromo.
Bromo also faces antitrust headwinds. Companies such as Germany's OHB and Spain's Indra worry that a merger of the three aerospace giants could reduce competition in the European satellite market. The EU competition chief has indicated that the project will not receive automatic approval simply because of its strategic significance.
From a business model perspective, Bromo is closer to a space equipment and systems supplier, while SpaceX and Starlink possess a complete business system from launch to network operations.
| Comparison Item | Bromo | SpaceX and Starlink | 
| Core Business | Satellite manufacturing, space systems, and related services | Rocket launch, satellite manufacturing, and LEO satellite internet | 
| Customer Base | Governments, military, European institutions, and enterprises | Individuals, enterprises, governments, and military | 
| Revenue Streams | Project orders, system integration, and long-term services | Launch services, satellite terminals, and broadband subscriptions | 
| Key Strengths | European industrial resources and government project experience | Launch frequency, satellite fleet scale, and network operation capabilities | 
| Current Status | Establishment and business integration yet to be completed | Has established a mature commercial satellite network | 
SpaceX's advantage lies in simultaneously mastering rocket launch, satellite production, and network operation capabilities. Starlink has established LEO satellite networks and user bases in multiple markets, while its higher launch frequency also helps lower satellite deployment costs.
Bromo currently has not announced a global LEO broadband network plan similar to Starlink, nor has it disclosed satellite numbers, user scale, or deployment timetables. Even if the project is approved, the new company still needs to address challenges such as mass satellite production, launch resources, terminal costs, network coverage, and long-term operations.
Therefore, Bromo's short-term competitive focus is more likely to center on European government communications, defense space, satellite manufacturing, and system integration projects, rather than directly competing for global commercial broadband users.
If the European Union and its member states increase support for European suppliers in government communications, defense aerospace, and critical infrastructure projects, SpaceX may face greater competitive pressure when participating in related projects. Bromo could also alter the allocation of orders in the European satellite manufacturing and system integration markets.
However, for Starlink's global business, the short-term impact remains limited. Bromo has yet to complete competition review and formal establishment, nor does it possess a network scale comparable to Starlink. SpaceX still boasts high launch frequencies, mature satellite production capabilities, and long-term operational experience.
Going forward, SpaceX investors should monitor three key developments: the outcome of the EU competition review, the final equity and business arrangements among the three companies, and whether public projects such as IRIS² can translate into actual orders.
In addition, whether the new company can establish stable satellite production and launch capabilities will also determine whether it can evolve from an industrial consolidation plan into a genuine commercial competitor.
Overall, Bromo may increase competitive pressure on SpaceX in European government space projects, but it is unlikely to weaken Starlink's global scale advantage in the short term.
Factors with a greater impact on SpaceX's long-term value remain Starlink's user growth, satellite launch efficiency, enterprise and government contracts, and changes in European spectrum and market access policies.

articles.title: Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role - Euronews
articles.summary: Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role  Euronews
articles.full_text:
Who controls the satellites on which armies rely? Reports of Starlink limits in Ukraine highlight the question. The EU is building IRIS², a 348-satellite network with a Bremen manufacturer.
This week, the Ukrainian army reported restrictions to the Starlink satellite service. The connection drops as soon as the receivers are travelling at more than 160 kilometres per hour, as is the case with drones.
The service was initially partially restored, but an upper limit remained in place. It is unclear who ordered the restriction.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk rejected responsibility that the company ordered the shutdown. Starshield is under the direct control of the US government, he wrote on X.
It is important to distinguish between the two systems: Starlink and Starshield are both developed by SpaceX but aimed at different customers. Starlink is the service for private and business users, Starshield is designed for governments and the military.
Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski reacted sharply on X, writing: "Hey, Elon Musk, you big man, are you once again playing politics with your products? As your European customers we are keeping a close eye on you."
Poland has paid for a large share of the Ukrainian terminals. This has once again raised the question of how dependent armed forces are on satellite links. Europe has therefore been working for some time on its own solution.
The European answer: IRIS²
The EU has been developing IRIS², its own satellite network, for around six years. The acronym stands for "Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite".
In German this roughly means infrastructure for resilience, connectivity and security via satellites. The system is intended to provide secure connections for governments, companies and citizens and to close mobile coverage gaps in Europe and Africa.
For encryption it will rely on quantum technology via the European quantum communication infrastructure EuroQCI.
In early August, the European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium agree on the implementation. The network will grow to 348 satellites, 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit.
A further 66 additional satellites are intended specifically to strengthen defence, security and emergency services. According to the Commission’s calculations, this will increase secured capacity for public-sector users by 60 percent in the EU and by 54 percent worldwide.
The focus is on states, the military and critical services; later on, private individuals are also to be able to use the network. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029. Initial services are to be introduced gradually from 2029 or 2030.
Germany's role
Germany is represented by the Bremen-based space company Orbitale Hochtechnologie Bremen (OHB).
On 31 August it signed a contract worth just under €1 billion with satellite operator SES for 18 satellites in medium Earth orbit for IRIS².
A single satellite weighs around 2.6 tonnes at launch. OHB chief executive Marco Fuchs sees the programme as an important step towards greater European independence.
Germany’s share of the project sparked disputes early on.
In December 2023, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs sent a strongly worded letter to the companies involved demanding urgent clarification of the German industry’s participation and its share in value creation, as reported by the Frankfurter Rundschau daily.
Bundeswehr: Its own satellite network?
Independently of IRIS², the Bundeswehr is planning its own satellite network. It is a national project financed by the federal government.
Major General Armin Fleischmann, the Bundeswehr’s space commissioner in the Cyber and Information Domain, told regional public broadcaster MDR that the plan is for a constellation similar to Starlink, only smaller.
He told the Handelsblatt business newspaper they wanted to have "flying Fritzboxes" in space. The network is initially to cover NATO’s eastern flank, under national control. Individual components will come from Western partners, including the United States.
As early as September 2025, defence minister Boris Pistorius announced at the space congress of the Federation of German Industries in Berlin that a total of €35 billion would be invested in military space projects by 2030. In July he visited OHB in Bremen to inspect satellite programmes and ongoing production.
The project is called SATCOMBw 4, short for satellite communication of the Bundeswehr. In its final expansion stage, according to the Bundeswehr, it is to comprise a three-digit number of satellites in low Earth orbit and cost between eight and ten billion euros. An initial partial constellation with up to 40 satellites is scheduled to be operational as early as 2029, with full operations planned from 2030.
The joint venture "OHB Rheinmetall Space Networks", based in Bremen, is bidding for the contract According to company information, OHB would be responsible for the satellites, Rheinmetall for the ground stations and end devices. No decision has yet been taken.
Industry reports suggest that the contract award could come around the turn of the year, though insiders consider early 2027 possible as well. OHB would then be involved in both major projects: in IRIS² as satellite manufacturer and in the Bundeswehr network as part of the joint venture.
Up to now, the Bundeswehr has been using two of its own satellites in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres altitude, COMSATBw-1 and COMSATBw-2, launched in 2009 and 2010.
Their successors are being built by Airbus and are scheduled to be handed over in orbit in 2029. The first of the three German radar satellites SARah was launched in 2022 on a Falcon 9 rocket from SpaceX.
Young Belgian company helping to build Europe’s satellite network
The satellites for IRIS² are being built by several companies. The largest share will not be supplied by an established group but by a young company:
Aerospacelab, founded in 2018 and based in Charleroi in Belgium, is building 264 satellites for low Earth orbit.
The order volume amounts to €2.4 billion, according to the company. The satellites are to be delivered by 2030. They will be produced in a new factory in Charleroi, where up to 500 satellites per year are to be built from 2027.
Airbus is building at least 66 satellites in the first layer for military communication, which are due to be ready in 2029. This means the entire low-orbit segment with 330 satellites has been allocated.
Together with the 18 OHB satellites for medium orbit, the network will comprise 348 satellites.
How realistic is 2029?
Whether the timetable can be met remains an open question. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029; according to media reports, the original plan was for them to go up two years earlier.
Experts view rocket launches as the bottleneck. Even the best satellites cannot reach space without rockets and those unable to launch them themselves remain dependent on others.
Europe is relying on the Ariane 6 launch vehicle, which has been lifting off into space since 2024. Andreas Knopp of the Bundeswehr University Munich points out in the weekly paper Das Parlament that the number of launches is limited, while political scientist Antje Nötzold of TU Chemnitz speaks in MDR of a "launcher problem."
So far this year, Ariane 6 has launched four times, three of those flights carrying satellites for Amazon Leo into orbit, the US company’s satellite internet service that is also intended to compete with Starlink.
Amazon has booked at least 18 Ariane 6 launches. In early August, the Commission named the procurement of launch services for IRIS² as one of the next steps.

articles.title: Google solves a major quantum computing problem, says it will bring us closer to practical quantum computers - India Today
articles.summary: Google solves a major quantum computing problem, says it will bring us closer to practical quantum computers  India Today
articles.full_text:
Google says it has found a way to reduce errors in its Willow quantum chip by 40 times, bringing practical quantum computers a step closer. The breakthrough could help these machines solve complex real-world problems, but more work is needed before they become a reality.
Google has made a big breakthrough in quantum computing that could bring practical quantum computers closer to reality. The company says it has found a way to reduce errors in its Willow quantum chip, the processor it uses for quantum computing, by around 40 times. In simple terms, this could help quantum computers solve complex problems more reliably, without wasting so much of their computing power on correcting errors.
Sharing the findings on X, CEO Sundar Pichai says the breakthrough is another step towards building quantum computers that can solve complex problems that even today's most powerful computers struggle with. “ Some magical progress towards "magic state" in quantum! Our GoogleQuantumAI team has demonstrated "magic state cultivation" on physical hardware for the first time. The result is a 40x error reduction on our Willow processor vs. previous methods, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.99% logical fidelity,” he wrote.
“It's another step towards useful, error-corrected quantum computers to help solve the hardest problems. The result is published in Science today, watch the video below to see how it works.”
So, what exactly has Google achieved, and why does it matter. Lets break it down.
What is the problem Google is trying to solve?
Quantum computers work differently from regular computers. They use tiny units of information called qubits, which are highly sensitive and can easily develop errors. This makes it difficult for quantum computers to carry out complex calculations accurately. Researchers are trying to reduce these errors so that quantum computers can solve real-world problems reliably.
One challenge is creating what scientists call “magic states”. These help quantum computers perform complex calculations. But each state is used up during a calculation, and any errors in it can affect the final result.
Until now, scientists have used a process called “distillation” to make these states more reliable by combining several imperfect ones. But this takes up a lot of computing power. According to Google some estimates suggest that producing these states could use up as much as 95 per cent of a quantum computer’s capacity, leaving little room for actual calculations.
However, Google has now demonstrated another approach, called “magic state cultivation”, on its quantum hardware. Researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty and Cody Jones developed the idea in 2024. 
Instead of relying on conventional distillation, this technique uses a series of checks to identify errors and reject faulty attempts, helping produce more reliable quantum states.
The process works a bit like a filter. It starts with an imperfect quantum state in a small area of the chip. The computer then runs a series of checks to identify errors and discard faulty attempts. States that pass these checks can be expanded across more qubits to create larger, more reliable states.
According to Google, getting the technique to work on real hardware took months of testing. Its researcher Emma Rosenfeld and her team found that changes in temperature and electrical equipment were interfering with their measurements. After fixing the issue, the team tested the technique using 54 of the 105 qubits in its Willow chip. Google says this reduced errors by around 40 times, with the resulting quantum states achieving 99.99 per cent logical fidelity. However, the process still rejected 92 per cent of attempts, meaning more work is needed before it can be used on a larger scale.
So, how will this help build real-world quantum computers? The idea is simple: if quantum computers can make reliable quantum states using fewer resources, they will have more computing power left to solve actual problems. This could eventually help researchers build larger quantum computers that can tackle complex tasks, such as studying molecules and developing new medicines, which are difficult for conventional computers to handle.
However, there is still a long way to go. Google says it still needs to show that the technique works on a much larger scale and that it can reduce errors enough for demanding calculations. For now, the breakthrough solves one important part of the puzzle, bringing the company a step closer to its goal of building quantum computers that can solve real-world problems.

Taiwan reportedly plans to raise billions of dollars to develop industrial parks in the US that would build a base for a comprehensive supply chain for Nvidia Corp. NVDA and other AI hardware makers in the country.
The initiative is starting with a complex in Texas that would cost as much as $4B to build, Bloomberg reported, citing Taiwan’s Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin.
The facilities would help smaller suppliers that are essential to the operations of Nvidia’s NVDA main production partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. TSM, and AI server assemblers, including Foxconn Technology Group (HNHPF) (HNHPF) to set up shop in the US, Kung said.

Taipei plans to add AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to a list of controlled items, Ming-hsin told Bloomberg News. “Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade,” Kung said in an interview on Oct. 12, referring to the trade deal that the US and Taiwan signed this year.
Taiwan-U.S. AI Investments Rise
The development comes as Quanta Computer (QUCCF) recently received approval to spend $973M to support assembling servers and peripheral equipment in Tennessee. And last month, Wistron WICOF was approved to spend $150M on a U.S. subsidiary that assembles circuit boards. It plans to spend another $146M to renovate a Texas plant.

The planned investment is separate from TSMC's (TSM) U.S. expansion. The world's largest contract chipmaker announced a further $100B investment in Arizona in July, bringing its total planned U.S. investment to $265B.
Nvidia NVDA relies on suppliers including TSMC TSM, SK hynix SKHY, Samsung Electronics SSNLF, and Micron Technology MU for chip manufacturing and memory, while its major customers include Microsoft MSFT, Amazon AMZN, and Meta Platforms META. articles.title: Google, major breakthrough in quantum computing - 36Kr
articles.summary: Google, major breakthrough in quantum computing  36Kr
articles.full_text:
Google, major breakthrough in quantum computing
   Google has verified a technology called "magic state cultivation" on its Willow processor, which has drastically reduced the quantum error rate.
Quantum computers are expected to deliver exponential computing power by processing multiple possibilities simultaneously. However, under current technical conditions, we are still far from reaching this ideal state.
   It is understood that in quantum computing, photons (or light particles) are used as qubits. When connected together, they deliver stronger processing capabilities than the binary 0 and 1 used by traditional computers. Qubits can be both 0 and 1 at the same time, in a superposition state, which enables them to process information much faster.
However, qubits are prone to frequent errors, so quantum computers still have limitations at present. To overcome these errors, the machines need to leverage so-called "magic states" — scientists at Google Research believe that the quantum chips they have developed may help achieve this goal.
The relevant study was published in the journal Science on Thursday. It is reported that Google verified a technology named "magic state cultivation" on its Willow processor, reducing the quantum error rate by about 40 times: without cultivation, around 4 out of every 1000 magic states are defective; after applying cultivation, only about 1 out of every 10,000 magic states is defective. The logical fidelity of the T state reaches 99.99%. This is the highest record in this field so far.
   "Magic states" are the key element to realize universal quantum computing. If a quantum processor wants to perform complex operations that outperform classical computers, it must rely on magic states to generate the required set of quantum operations. However, magic states cannot be reused once used, making them a scarce resource. Moreover, generating magic states with a sufficiently low error rate has long been a major challenge in building practical large-scale systems.
Furthermore, an even greater challenge lies in production cost. Some research estimates show that quantum computers may need to devote up to 95% of their total computing power to magic state production, leaving extremely scarce resources for actual computing tasks. This bottleneck was foreseen by researchers as early as 2004. In the following two decades, the academic community has continuously explored methods to reduce the production cost of magic states, but progress has been slow.
In the aforementioned new study, researchers demonstrated how to use a horticulture-inspired technique called "cultivation" to deliver magic states at lower costs.
The research results provide experimental verification for the theoretical method proposed in 2024. At that time, Google Quantum AI researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty and Cody Jones proposed the magic state cultivation scheme on the basis of existing literature.
Its core idea is to design the magic state production process as a set of "filtering mechanism": Google uses synergistic measurement to detect errors and filter out invalid attempts, so as to generate higher-quality quantum states with fewer resources.
And the latest research confirms that on the Willow supercomputer, this method achieves a logical fidelity of 99.99% for the T state (a special quantum state used in quantum computing), setting a new record in this field.
Besides reducing errors, Google's researchers also proved that purified quantum states can be transferred between two different error correction methods, which marks the progress of this technology in terms of integration into Google's existing architecture.
However, despite the above progress, Google also made it clear that further research is needed to extend this technology to the field of practical quantum computing, but these findings provide a potential way to reduce the hardware resources required to build a fault-tolerant quantum system.
This article is from the WeChat official account "Sci-Tech Innovation Board Daily", written by Huang Junzhi, and published with authorization by 36Kr.

articles.title: Takafumi Horie Calls for Japan to Build Independent Satellite Communications Network, Warning Against U.S. Dependence - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Takafumi Horie Calls for Japan to Build Independent Satellite Communications Network, Warning Against U.S. Dependence  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Entrepreneur Takafumi Horie expressed his view on October 15 via his YouTube channel that Japan should possess its own satellite communications network. Citing the reported speed restrictions imposed on SpaceX's military satellite communications service "Starshield" in Ukraine, he emphasized the national security risks of depending on foreign companies' communications infrastructure.
The focal point of the issue is a restriction that prevents drones equipped with Starshield terminals from maintaining communications when traveling faster than 160 kilometers per hour. Horie noted that this restriction "effectively amounts to crippling Ukraine's drones." He voiced concern over a structure in which even allied nations' communications usage can be dictated by U.S. decisions, stating that "relying on American companies is extremely dangerous."
Starshield is a military and intelligence satellite system developed by SpaceX for the U.S. Department of Defense. Built on the foundation of Starlink's commercial broadband network, it offers higher-security communications through enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals. Elon Musk explained in a post on X (formerly Twitter) on October 14 that Starshield is owned and controlled by the U.S. government, with speed and usage restrictions determined by the U.S. military or the U.S. president.
Horie took issue with this structure and expressed the view that each region needs its own low-Earth orbit satellite communications network. For Japan, he argued that "Japan should build its own independent system."
Interstellar Technologies, the space development company where Horie serves as a director, is precisely aiming to realize this vision. The company's satellite initiative "Our Stars" seeks to launch large numbers of ultra-small satellites to deliver high-speed, high-capacity communications that connect directly to smartphones, automobiles, and other devices.
At the core of this effort is technology that uses electromagnets to control the relative positioning of microsatellites. Even though individual satellites are small, the concept envisions flying them in formation as a "swarm" that functions collectively as one large antenna. In March 2026, the company announced it had completed initial verification of this control technology through simulations and ground-based experiments.
Building a satellite communications network requires placing numerous satellites into orbit, making launch capability essential. The company is accelerating the commercialization of its small rocket "ZERO" while also having begun design work on a future large rocket "DECA," pursuing faster launch timelines and lower costs in parallel.
The Boundary Between Starlink and Starshield
Ukraine's complaints have drawn renewed attention to the relationship between the two systems: Starlink and Starshield. While Musk describes them as separate entities, in practice they often share the same satellite technology.
Starlink is SpaceX's primary revenue generator, a satellite internet network comprising more than 11,000 satellites. It delivers broadband directly to terminals roughly the size of a folded newspaper and serves approximately 13 million subscribers. Since launching its first satellites aboard reusable rockets in 2019, it has provided faster connections from low-Earth orbit than traditional communications satellites.
Starshield is the military version that leverages Starlink's technology, engineering, and operational experience. Beyond secure communications, it is said to offer payload capabilities for Earth observation and sensors. Its largest customer, the U.S. Department of Defense, has invested billions of dollars in both Starlink and Starshield services. Reuters reported in 2024 that the Pentagon has also purchased communications satellites for ballistic missile warning and a reconnaissance satellite constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office.
The boundary between the two systems remains ambiguous. SpaceX announced Starshield in late 2022 after Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine, but the high level of secrecy surrounding national security space programs has kept the precise delineation opaque.
This distinction also became a point of contention in early 2026 when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over price increases for satellite communications for military drones amid the Iran situation. SpaceX argued that some customers paying approximately $5,000 (about ¥790,000) per Starlink terminal should have been using Starshield, which costs approximately $25,000 (about ¥4 million) per terminal.
Expansion to Allied Nations and Japan's Choices
Starshield adoption extends beyond the United States. The United Kingdom has also introduced the system, operating it through dedicated terminals and independent network gateways while using the same satellite constellation, ground stations, and ground infrastructure as Starlink. New Zealand is also conducting trial operations to assess its utility for military operations.
Horie's argument is set against the reality that this U.S.-led satellite communications network now extends to allied nations. As the speed restrictions in Ukraine demonstrated, the fact that communications availability can change based on a single U.S. government decision represents a risk factor that even allies cannot ignore.
Japan has historically relied heavily on U.S. capabilities for satellite communications in the security domain. Meanwhile, moves by private companies like Interstellar Technologies to build independent satellite communications networks could offer an alternative to this dependency structure. The technology of flying numerous small satellites in formation to create a single communications network has the potential to reduce launch costs compared to conventional large satellites, drawing attention as a realistic approach for Japan to establish its own low-Earth orbit communications network.
That said, many challenges remain before practical implementation, including establishing launch capability, frequency allocation, and international coordination. Horie's remarks present both a demonstration of technological possibility and a policy question about how to secure autonomy in national security.

articles.title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
articles.summary: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. articles.full_text:
I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it.



What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.



There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?





There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis, and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats.



I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it.



That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though.



I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin.



Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?”





Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced.



Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor, a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider.



With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero. Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated. As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.”



I miss Peppy. But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not.



RIP to the one and only Peppy.
